♻ ☆ Understanding and Learning Prediction Targets in Diffusion Models
Qing Jin, Chaoyang Wang
Recent advances in diffusion and flow matching models have highlighted a shift in the preferred prediction target -- moving from noise ($\varepsilon$) and velocity (v) to direct data (x) prediction -- particularly in high-dimensional settings. However, a formal explanation of why the optimal target depends on the specific properties of the data remains elusive. In this work, we provide a theoretical framework based on a generalized prediction formulation $u=kx-(1-k)n$, where $x$ represents clean data and $n$ denotes noise. This formulation accommodates arbitrary targets, of which $\varepsilon$-, v-, and x-prediction are special cases. We derive the analytical relationship between data's geometry and the optimal prediction target, offering a rigorous justification for why x-prediction becomes superior when the ambient dimension significantly exceeds the data's intrinsic dimension. Furthermore, our controlled analysis reveals how time conditioning and loss variations systematically modulate this optimal objective. While our theory identifies dimensionality as the governing factor for the optimal prediction target, the intrinsic dimension of manifold-bound data is typically intractable to estimate in practice. To bridge this gap, we propose k-Diff, a framework that employs a data-driven approach to learn the optimal prediction parameter k directly from data, bypassing the need for explicit dimension estimation. Extensive experiments in both latent-space and pixel-space image generation demonstrate that k-Diff consistently outperforms fixed-target baselines across varying architectures and data scales, providing a principled and automated approach to enhancing generative performance.

PBV constructs critics from pairwise candidate differences, on the log scale for occupancy ratios, and selects the candidate with the smallest worst-case penalized score. This construction approximates oracle critics given by $Q$-function errors and log ratios of candidate to true occupancy ratios, whose Bellman and adjoint Bellman moments control estimation error. Critic penalties account for approximation error under candidate-class misspecification. On Hopper and DeepOPE, unweighted PBV is competitive with LSTD-Tournament, often achieving higher accuracy on Hopper, while importance weighting can further improve performance under controlled overlap.

By minimizing the residual locally on overlapping patches, we bypass the global implicit solve inherent to fixed discretizations, which slows time- and space-stepping and complicates learning. Our method scales linearly with domain size via Jacobi iteration, and places no structural requirements on the learned network, allowing it to be coupled with existing physics-guided machine learning (ML) methods. We validate our approach on a learned representation of a double pendulum, a one-dimensional wave equation, and a two-dimensional wave equation. Coupled with structured sparsity, this yields highly efficient weight decompositions without sacrificing functional fidelity. Across diverse architectures, scales, and modalities, our method achieves state-of-the-art results, consistently outperforming independent structured weight decompositions and alternative pairwise weight factorizations, which operate under heuristic grouping strategies. The Blum-Gladyshev ($\mathsf{BG}$-0) noise model instead allows the stochastic gradient variance to grow quadratically with the distance from the initialization and has recently been identified as the weakest known viable variance assumption. We further extend our analysis to the symmetric generalized smoothness framework, which captures objectives whose local curvature can scale with the gradient norm. To our knowledge, these are the first convergence guarantees for normalized methods in nonconvex stochastic optimization under $\mathsf{BG}$-0 noise without bounded domains.

We study AI alignment through the lens of law-and-economics models of deterrence and enforcement. In these models, misconduct is not treated as an external failure, but as a strategic response to incentives: an actor weighs the gain from violation against the probability of detection and the severity of punishment. We argue that the same logic arises naturally in agentic AI pipelines. A solver may benefit from producing a persuasive but incorrect answer, hiding uncertainty, or exploiting spurious shortcuts, while an auditor or verifier must decide whether costly monitoring is worthwhile. Alignment is therefore a fixed-point problem: stronger penalties may deter solver misbehavior, but they can also reduce the auditor's incentive to inspect, since auditing then mainly incurs cost on a population that appears increasingly aligned. This perspective also changes what should count as a post-training signal. Standard feedback often attaches reward to the final answer alone, but a solver-auditor pipeline exposes the full correction event: whether the solver erred, whether the auditor inspected, whether the error was caught, and whether oversight incentives remained active. We formalize this interaction in a two-agent model in which a principal chooses rewards over joint correction outcomes, inducing both solver behavior and auditor monitoring. Reward design is therefore a bilevel optimization problem: rewards are judged not by their immediate semantic meaning, but by the behavioral equilibrium they induce. We propose a bandit-based outer-loop procedure for searching over reward profiles using noisy interaction feedback. Experiments on an LLM coding pipeline show that adaptive reward profiles can maintain useful oversight pressure and improve principal-aligned outcomes relative to static hand-designed rewards, including a substantial reduction in hallucinated incorrect attempts.

♻ ☆ A Tutorial on Gaussian Process Learning-based Model Predictive Control
Jie Wang, Youmin Zhang
This tutorial provides an accessible and implementation-oriented introduction to Gaussian process learning-based model predictive control (GP-MPC), which combines probabilistic residual modeling with receding-horizon control. Its central tutorial contribution is a detailed, step-by-step derivation of multi-step mean and covariance propagation for GP-augmented prediction models. The derivation shows how commonly used propagation formulas follow from the laws of total expectation and total covariance, and clarifies the roles of the GP posterior mean, GP posterior covariance, uncertain inputs, and query-output cross-covariances. Building on this foundation, the article distinguishes mean-only unconstrained GP predictive control from uncertainty-aware constrained GP-MPC, clarifies regulation and output-tracking formulations, and provides concise implementation and computational-complexity guidance, including practical software-tool references and discussion of the scope of closed-loop guarantees. Mobile-robot path-following examples illustrate mean-only unconstrained implementations, whereas mixed-vehicle platooning illustrates uncertainty-aware constrained GP-MPC with uncertainty-dependent safety-distance tightening. The tutorial is intended to help researchers and practitioners understand, implement, and critically evaluate GP-MPC designs for robotic and autonomous systems operating under modeling uncertainty.

♻ ☆ Domain-Routed Delta Optimization for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
Lin Yao
Multi-teacher on-policy distillation can yield uneven domain capabilities. We propose Domain-Routed Delta Optimization (DRD-MOPD), composing a frozen base with expert-initialized trainable deltas. Domains update their deltas with independent optimizer states and clipping. After joint training, Post-separate exports the base plus one trained delta per domain, selected by known task domain without retraining. Using AdamW, the unweighted full student reaches 32.83% Macro across six benchmarks after 20 updates, versus 32.21% for a matched shared control. Post-separate raises Macro with Open-MOPD weighting.
♻ ☆ Convergence and stability of Q-learning in Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
Massimiliano Manenti, Andrea Iannelli
Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning promises, among other benefits, to efficiently capture and utilize the temporal structure of a decision-making problem and to enhance transfer learning capabilities, but theoretical guarantees lag behind practice. In this paper, we propose a Feudal Q-learning scheme and investigate under which conditions its coupled updates converge and are stable. By leveraging the theory of Stochastic Approximation and the ODE method, we present a theorem stating the convergence and stability properties of Feudal Q-learning. This provides a principled convergence and stability analysis tailored to Feudal RL. Moreover, we show that the updates converge to a point that can be interpreted as an equilibrium of a suitably defined game, opening the door to game-theoretic approaches to Hierarchical RL. Lastly, experiments based on the Feudal Q-learning algorithm support the outcomes anticipated by theory.
♻ ☆ Probabilistic Signature Inversion: Learning Conditional Distributions from Truncated Signatures NeurIPS 2026
Junoh Kang, Kiseop Lee, Bohyung Han
The signature transform is a principled feature map for continuous-time paths, valued for its uniqueness and universality. Recovering a path from its truncated signature is, however, structurally ill-posed, because the truncated signature map is not injective. We therefore reframe truncated signature inversion as a probabilistic problem---learning the conditional distribution of a path given its truncated signature---and adopt a signature-conditioned flow matching model as a practical estimator. This formulation elucidates the fundamental difficulty of inversion: posterior-sampling reconstruction error quantifies the irreducible uncertainty remaining after conditioning on a statistic. For Gaussian process families, we derive this error from the tractable posterior under linear-statistics conditioning, obtaining a closed form for log-GBM and numerically tractable formulas for drifted fBM and OU. This oracle error upper-bounds the corresponding error under truncated-signature conditioning, since truncated signatures are more informative than linear statistics. The experimental results are consistent with the theoretical analysis: the learned sampler under linear-statistics conditioning closely matches the theoretically derived posterior in both reconstruction error and distribution, while reconstruction errors decrease under richer truncated-signature conditioning. Moreover, generated paths faithfully recover the conditioning signature and preserve key distributional and temporal structures. Together, these results establish a well-posed probabilistic framework for truncated-signature inversion, with applicability demonstrated on financial data beyond the process families covered by theory. Code is available at https://github.com/Junoh-Kang/ProbSigInv.

♻ ☆ Learning Where to Simulate: Generative Active Sampling for Online PDE Surrogate Training
Pierre Cesar, Sofya Dymchenko, Abhishek Purandare, Bruno Raffin
Paper published at NeurIPS 2026. For data-driven PDE surrogates, generalizing across a wide range of initial conditions and physical coefficients requires a training set of numerical simulations that consistently covers the resulting dynamics. Yet uniform sampling of these configuration parameters can leave challenging regimes insufficiently covered, leading to high prediction errors and large error variance in the trained surrogate. To address this sampling imbalance, we introduce the Online Generative Active Sampling (OGAS), which continuously adapts configuration sampling during surrogate training, as an alternative to classical round-based active learning. As the surrogate learns from a stream of simulation data generated online, OGAS trains a fast diffusion model in parallel to sample configuration parameters conditioned on a training difficulty signal, such as loss or uncertainty. This conditional sampler enables OGAS to parametrize subsequent simulations to generate challenging training data by prioritizing configurations with high difficulty values. We evaluate OGAS on 2D PDEs with distinct challenging dynamics-Kuramoto--Sivashinsky, Navier--Stokes, and Gray--Scott-using multiple surrogate architectures and up to 308 configuration parameters. Across the tested PDEs and architectures, OGAS consistently reduces the 99th-percentile prediction error and overall error dispersion compared with uniform sampling, while wall-clock overhead is negligible. Code and experiments are available at https://github.com/melissa-sa/ogas.

☆ Sketching Language Models for Context Attribution
Christopher Liaw, Aranyak Mehta, Grigoris Velegkas, Felix Zhou
Context attribution asks how removing parts of a prompt changes a language model's output. We study leave-one-out (LOO) attribution for a prompt of $n$ tokens and a fixed measurement function. Computing all LOO values directly requires $n$ model evaluations. Under a stability assumption, our algorithm estimates all LOO values to error proportional to $\varepsilon$ with constant probability using $O(\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}/\varepsilon)$ evaluation calls. To complement our upper bound, we prove a matching $Ω(\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}/\varepsilon)$ lower bound on the number of evaluation calls in an oracle model. Empirically, we verify coefficient decay consistent with stability and evaluate the performance of our sketching algorithm on a small language-model retrieval task. Technically, our result is based on a sketching algorithm for arithmetic circuits whose Taylor coefficients satisfy the stability condition recently introduced by Gunn [Gun26]. A direct adaptation of their forward differentiation sketches would require $\widetilde{O}(\log(n)/\varepsilon^2)$ evaluation calls. Our key observation is that we can apply forward differentiation to the backpropagation circuit, with only constant overhead over a forward sketch of the same Taylor degree. This reduces the variance of the sketches and is key to our improved evaluation bound. Our lower bound builds on the techniques of Amsel, Chen, Duman Keles, Halikias, Musco, and Musco [ACDH+26, SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications] for lower bounding the number of matrix-vector queries to estimate the diagonal elements of random matrices.

The short duration of general insurance contracts leads to rapid distributional shifts in the data, warranting regular model updates. This process may yield a post-update model that differs considerably from the pre-update model in both predictions and structure. Structural stability is upstream of predictive stability, yet existing structural stability metrics are mostly restricted to simple decision trees. Thus, we first introduce the notion of functional transparency, characterising models with a prediction function that can be expressed as a sum of univariate functions for main effects and bivariate functions for pairwise interactions. Then, we propose the Mean Squared Shape function distance, a metric to quantify the structural stability of functionally transparent models, which are particularly relevant in actuarial science. Using three public auto insurance datasets, we present a benchmark study to demonstrate the usefulness of our metric in identifying a stable and accurate transparent model. Generalised linear models with centred numerical covariates are stable, and explainable boosting machines (EBMs) offer a compromise between stability and performance. We also find that stabilisation strategies, such as sequential modelling and fixed hyperparameters, can substantially improve stability for both EBM and XGBoost models, with negligible impact on performance.

☆ Linear Regression with Self-Selection Bias in Polynomial Time
Felix Zhou
We revisit the problem of estimating $k$ linear regressors with self-selection bias in $n$ dimensions up to error $\varepsilon$ with the maximum self-selection criterion, as introduced by Cherapanamjeri, Daskalakis, Ilyas, and Zampetakis [CDIZ23, STOC]. Our main result is a $\mathrm{poly}(n,k,1/\varepsilon)$ time algorithm for the unknown-index variant of this problem, thereby improving upon the running times of the best known algorithms due to Gaitonde and Mossel [GM24] and Kalavasis, Mehrotra, and Zhou [KMZ26, COLT] with exponential dependence on $k$. Our algorithm succeeds in the presence of correlated noise between regressors, which captures the related setting of max-affine regression. Consequently, we also give the first polynomial-time algorithm for this problem, improving on the prior works of Ghosh, Pananjady, Guntuboyina, and Ramchandran [GPGR22, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory] and Gaitonde and Mossel [GM24] with exponential dependence on $k$. Prior works exhaustively search over a $k$-dimensional subspace spanned by the regressors, using conditional moments of the response to test candidates. In contrast, our algorithm is driven by an improved understanding of the moments of the covariates. We show that, restricting to observations with large response values, the degree-$(\log n)$ Hermite moment of the covariates approximately decomposes as a sum of tensor powers of the regressors. The first step of our algorithm can be viewed as a tensor decomposition algorithm for these implicitly represented high-order tensors, which outputs unit vectors parallel to the regressors. A secondary step based on a simple variant of ordinary least squares extracts estimates for the regressors given these unit vectors. We believe our analytic insight and algorithmic components may have applications to designing efficient algorithms for other latent-variable problems.
☆ Introducing Feedback Delays to Non-Delayed Adversarial MDPs: Optimal $\sqrt S$ and $\sqrt K$ Dependencies in Tabular and Linear AMDPs
Aarush Kulkarni, Khang Nguyen, William Chang, Yan Dai
We study regret minimization in episodic Adversarial Markov Decision Processes (AMDPs) with unknown transitions and bandit feedback. In tabular AMDPs with $S$ states, $A$ actions, and horizon $H$, the best known $K$-episode regret is $\tilde O(HS\sqrt{AK})$, whose $\sqrt S$ gap to the $Ω(H\sqrt{SAK})$ lower bound has long remained open. In linear AMDPs with $d$-dimensional features, after a five-year line of improvements starting from $K^{14/15}$, computationally efficient algorithms without a simulator or exploratory assumptions still only attain $\tilde O(K^{3/4})$ regret. A common challenge in both settings is to estimate the Q-function of a changing policy: past data comes from earlier policies that differ from (and are correlated with) the current one, while freezing the policy for future episodes worsens the dependency on $K$. We instead propose a general technique called introduced feedback delays: we estimate the Q-function of the policy using future episodes while still updating the policy, as if the feedback were delayed. While feedback delays are usually an obstacle imposed by the environment, here they are introduced voluntarily and, perhaps surprisingly, come at no extra cost. We develop Geometric Resampling with Rejection (GRR) to account for policy changes during the delay, and threshold the visitation probabilities to avoid long delays on rarely visited state-action pairs. With this unified technique, our policy optimization algorithms achieve, with high probability, $\tilde O(\text{poly}(H)\sqrt{SAK})$ regret in tabular AMDPs, resolving the open problem; and $\tilde O(\text{poly}(d,H)\sqrt K)$ regret in linear AMDPs, giving the first efficient algorithm optimal in $K$. They also naturally extend to delayed AMDPs with a total feedback delay $\mathfrak D$, yielding the first bounds optimal in $S$ and $\mathfrak D$ (tabular) and in $K$ and $\mathfrak D$ (linear).
☆ Disentangling Spurious Correlations: How IRM Handles Diverse Shortcuts in Text Classification EMNLP 2026
Paul Grunenwald, Benoît Crabbé, Guillaume Wisniewski, Pirmin Lemberger
In NLP, models trained via Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) often exploit spurious correlations, such as dialectal markers, at the expense of robust linguistic features, thereby degrading their out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) aims to suppress such shortcuts by identifying predictive relationships that remain stable across environments, but its practical utility for NLP remains debated. We use a causality-driven framework to evaluate IRM under three shortcut-generating mechanisms: label-generated features, confounding, and selection bias. Our results show that IRM successfully rejects shortcuts across the evaluated causal and anti-causal structures, including under limited environmental variation and increasing label noise. We then extend our analysis beyond controlled synthetic artifacts to two less constrained settings: gender-profession associations in Bias in Bios and semantically loaded actor-name shortcuts in ActorCorr. These experiments show that invariant learning can mitigate more realistic textual shortcuts, while semantically meaningful features require careful calibration of the invariance penalty.

☆ Prevalence Bounds for Edited Watermarked Text: Power Envelopes and Calibration Sensitivity

We study this share for Gumbel-max and green-list (KGW) watermarks when every document may have been edited by an unknown amount. Without restrictions on the edits, the upper end of the identified set is 1. Combining a known least-favourable next-token distribution with a sequential coupling, we derive a power envelope indexed by three budgets: a retention floor, an entropy budget, and a budget for in-place substitutions, which for Gumbel-max make edited positions look less watermarked than human text. The envelope gives an identified set that is sharp for the alternatives it dominates, finite-sample bounds on the realized share of a fixed corpus with either the exact null or a null calibrated on an independent human sample, and confidence sequences for streams. In Gumbel-max simulations where the envelope binds, the bounds cover, and the threshold that maximizes the gap between envelope and null is generally as tight as twelve thresholds. On text from OPT-1.3B and Qwen3-1.7B, 12,000 fresh human documents scored under three keys show no robust departure from the exact null, and all bounds covered in resampling trials from finite pools of documents with random edits, substitutions and paraphrases; at a share of 0.2 the exact-null bound is about [0.14,0.38]. These results are fragile in two ways we make precise. LLM-paraphrased KGW pools fall below the envelope, yet at 2000 documents the bounds still covered in these trials. A simulated null error of 0.01, comparable to the largest deviation we observed at our thresholds, is likewise harmless at 2000 documents but breaks exact-null coverage at 100,000; a null calibrated on an independent human sample keeps coverage there, but needs a large reference sample to stay narrow.

☆ Temporal Regularized Learning: Self-Supervised Learning Local in Space and Time
Davide Wiest
Layer-local self-supervised objectives remove the backward pass between layers, but almost all still compute their loss over a batch of samples and are therefore local in space but not in time. We introduce Temporal Regularized Learning (TeReL), a spatially and temporally local learning rule for self-supervised representation learning from sequential input streams. The key idea is to instantiate a VICReg-style objective with temporally adjacent positives and non-differentiated running population statistics, yielding a per-neuron online loss with bounded state. The objective is a soft form of Slow Feature Analysis, and its gradient is a Hebbian update of the feedforward weights and an anti-Hebbian update of one lateral matrix per layer. The aim of the experiments is to show that the rule works in a small network, not to compete with backpropagation. On a class-chunked MNIST stream, a two-layer fully connected network trained with batch size one outperforms random features (96.48% versus 95.09% linear-probe accuracy) and classical SFA, and a variant that relaxes both locality constraints is comparable to supervised backpropagation. Because training and inference use the same computation, the network can keep learning from unlabeled data during inference without loss of accuracy.

☆ Entire sig-jump-diffusions, their expected signature and applications to score-based generative modeling
Christa Cuchiero, Francesca Primavera, Sara Svaluto-Ferro

These are semimartingales whose characteristics are given by linear combinations of potentially infinitely many components of their own signature. We show that their expected signature can be computed by solving linear ODEs in the extended tensor algebra, providing a tractable foundation for learning procedures. Specifically, the learning of a generalized score function for jump diffusions, a key ingredient of our generative modeling framework, can be reduced to solving linear ODEs and a deterministic optimization problem. We further prove that polynomial jump-diffusions can be embedded into this framework, and that their expected signature reduces to a finite-dimensional system of linear ODEs. Building on this result, we develop an alternative approach for finite-dimensional data, based on inverse signature matching, a method that learns the score by matching the expected signature of the reverse process with that of the inverse forward signature.

A large body of work in quantum machine learning has centered on characterizing the expressivity and performance of quantum models. In contrast, little attention has been paid to the reliability of predictions beyond average performance measures such as accuracy. In this work, we introduce an uncertainty-aware quantum classification framework based on Dempster-Shafer theory. This theory allows to express uncertainty through weights assigned not only to individual classification labels but to sets of labels. We introduce a training strategy that enables parameterized quantum circuits to learn such assignments directly from data. This provides an efficient way to prepare the corresponding quantum states and enables the application of different post-processing strategies. In particular, it offers a practical setting for quantum Dempster-Shafer fusion procedures with polynomial resource requirements, even when the corresponding mass functions are defined over exponentially many subsets. Overall, our work represents a step toward enabling quantum models to express uncertainty about their predictions, thereby extending the evaluation of quantum models beyond predictive performance alone.

Exact Bayes energy posteriors supply numerical gap estimates for specified bases. Additional bounds relate feature compression, independently learned mode spans and sensor-noise error to log loss. ☆ On the Difficulty of Sequence-Level Supervised Learning for Autoregressive Language Models
Mathieu Blondel, Michaël E. Sander, Germain Vivier-Ardisson, Tianlin Liu, Vincent Roulet
During the supervised learning phase, autoregressive language models are typically trained by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of the training data, which decomposes as a sum of token-level cross-entropies via teacher forcing. This objective is simple and efficient but potentially suffers from so-called exposure bias: a mismatch between the way the model is trained and the way it is used at inference time. Can we instead design sequence-level loss functions that incorporate inference-time decoding procedures, such as greedy decoding or autoregressive sampling? We show that two natural attempts lead to loss functions that are fundamentally flawed: unbounded below. We further show that these two flawed loss functions are intimately connected: using autoregressive Gumbel tricks, the sampling based loss is the expected greedy loss under Gumbel perturbations. Since the pathology stems from the dependence of the decoded sequence on the model parameters, we analyze the update direction obtained by applying a stop gradient on the sampling procedure, leading to a moment matching direction. While it is not the gradient of any loss function, we prove that it defines a valid descent direction in function space for the autoregressive negative log-likelihood. Despite these theoretical insights, the moment matching direction suffers from high variance. We conclude that teacher forcing may well be ``all you need'' for supervised learning of autoregressive models.

This tradeoff yields a regime-dependent comparison with SGD: (i) SignSGD achieves improved data efficiency in the hard-task regime; (ii) both optimizers achieve the same data efficiency in the easy-task regime, but SignSGD maintains this efficiency at larger batch sizes, requiring fewer optimization steps for a fixed data budget. LLM pre-training experiments further suggest that the SignSGD FSL better captures the batch-size dependence of loss dynamics for sign-based optimizers than the original SGD FSL.

However, training Gaussian processes (GPs) has a computational cost of $O(n^3)$, while the memory and prediction costs are also $O(n^2)$. In this work, we propose a class of approximations based on sparse covariance matrices, where the kernel matrix is sparsified according to the spatial proximity of the design points. We analyze the accuracy of the resulting approximate posterior distribution and show that the proposed approach preserves optimal statistical inference properties, provided that the dependencies among a sufficient number of neighboring points for each feature are retained. We derive explicit sufficient and necessary conditions on the number of neighbors required in a general setting and apply these results to standard kernels, including the squared exponential and Matérn kernels. Our theoretical findings are supported by numerical experiments.

These experiments show that persistent latent-conditioned adaptation can support sequential inference when earlier evidence is absent from the decoder context.

Empirically, we show that the proposed framework outperforms direct criterion-specific methods in multiple settings and further evaluate it on the ACTG175 HIV clinical trial, a randomized study comparing several antiretroviral regimens in HIV-infected adults.

Holding out one country at a time, we construct external-validity intervals for the held-out country from the remaining source sites and show how our framework connects different extrapolation assumptions to concrete partial identification bounds.

☆ Gradient Flows over Convex Bodies for Learning Optimal Regularizers

We consider the question of describing gradient flows over the collection of convex bodies. This is motivated by foundational questions arising in inverse problems. Suppose we wish to solve an ill-posed inverse problem using regularization techniques. Can we learn an optimal choice of a convex regularizer directly from prior data? Given a numerical algorithm that computes such an optimal regularizer, is there a principled manner for describing the evolution of its iterates? The objective of this paper is to lay the foundation towards answering these questions. To this end, we consider a criterion of an optimal regularizer based on seeking a convex body that minimizes the expected gauge evaluation with respect to a prior data distribution subject to a volume constraint. The formulation is initially nonconvex, but admits hidden convexity by passing to its polar. We characterize the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions that certify global optimality. We also analyze the $L^2$-gradient flow as well as a minimizing movement scheme with the Hausdorff penalty. Our results show that the objective gap decays exponentially along the gradient flow and we obtain dimension-dependent rates for both the objective gap and distance to the optimal body for the Hausdorff scheme. Finally, we apply the KKT conditions to identify explicit optimal convex bodies. For data where the optimal nonconvex regularizer is the $\ell_p$-quasinorm, $p \in (0,1)$, the optimal convex regularizer is the volume-normalized $\ell_1$-ball. For data described by paired basis atoms, the optimal convex regularizer is the polar of a shifted zonotope.

Within this setting, the results show accurate classification across simulated and experimental data, improved alignment between the two domains, and reduced forgetting compared with naïve fine-tuning. Predictive uncertainty is also evaluated on unfamiliar and noisy inputs. The contribution is the integration and evaluation of these capabilities for sequential XRD interpretation. In this paper, we present a flow-based method for global optimization of continuous Sobolev functions, called Stein Boltzmann Sampling (SBS). SBS initializes uniformly a number of particles representing candidate solutions, then uses the Stein Variational Gradient Descent (SVGD) algorithm to sequentially and deterministically move those particles in order to approximate a target distribution whose mass is concentrated around promising areas of the domain of the optimized function. The target is chosen to be a properly parametrized Boltzmann distribution. A detailed comparison with state-of-the-art methods on benchmark functions demonstrates that SBS and its variants are highly competitive, while the combination of the two variants provides the best trade-off between accuracy and computational cost.

In this work we study this question in distributional reinforcement learning, where the learned return distribution P_θ(Z | s,a) can be compared directly with an environment-grounded distribution P_env(Z | s,a) estimated by snapshot-restart Monte Carlo. Our audit first screens for the claims that a risk-sensitive user would act upon, using the excess Wasserstein gap between the top two actions (which is equal to the mass by which first-order stochastic dominance is violated). Each claim is then tested against ground truth using permutation nulls, bootstrap refutation and FDR control. Across QR-DQN, C51 and IQN on MinAtar (33 runs), 40-95% of the strongest claimed risk trade-offs are refuted at 95% confidence, their placement is statistically indistinguishable from a truth-blind placement, and almost none of them can be confirmed. A similar pattern is seen for a pretrained full-Atari QR-DQN. On positive controls of known magnitude the same audit confirms 96-100% of real claims (correlation 0.89-0.92), so it is able to detect real risk when it is present. Acting on the learned CVaR advice at the most-flagged states gives results ranging from beneficial to significantly worse than chance. Ensembling, risk-sensitive training and recalibration do not fix the problem, and the recalibration experiment indicates that the learned spread has no usable information about the true risk. For the latter, we specifically consider the use of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. We demonstrate the benefits of reduced error in various applied models.

The bootstrap is a standard tool for uncertainty quantification because of its broad applicability. As increasingly large datasets become available, such as the 2023 U.S. Natality data from the National Vital Statistics System (NVSS), which includes 3,605,081 registered births (of which 2,980,739 form our analytic sample after cohort restrictions), the computational demands of these methods increase substantially. Kernel methods are known to scale poorly with sample size, and this limitation is further exacerbated by the repeated re-fitting required by the bootstrap. As a result, bootstrap-based inference for kernel-based estimators can become computationally infeasible in large-scale settings. In this paper, we address these challenges by extending the causal Bag of Little Bootstraps (cBLB) algorithm of Kosko et al. (2023) to kernel methods. Our approach achieves computational scalability by combining subsampling and resampling while preserving first-order uncertainty quantification and asymptotically correct coverage. We evaluate the method across three representative implementations: kernelized augmented outcome-weighted learning, kernel-based minimax weighting, and double machine learning with kernel support vector machines. We show in simulations that our method yields confidence intervals with nominal coverage at a fraction of the computational cost. We further demonstrate its utility in a real-world application by estimating the effect of any amount of smoking on birth weight, as well as the optimal treatment regime, using the NVSS dataset, where the standard bootstrap is prohibitively expensive computationally and effectively infeasible at this scale.

♻ ☆ Adversarial Attacks on Downstream Weather Forecasting Models: Application to Tropical Cyclone Trajectory Prediction
Yue Deng, Francisco Santos, Pang-Ning Tan, Lifeng Luo
Deep learning-based weather forecasting (DLWF) models leverage past weather observations to generate future forecasts, supporting a wide range of downstream applications, including tropical cyclone (TC) prediction. In this paper, we investigate the vulnerability of these models to adversarial attacks, where subtle perturbations to upstream forecasts can alter downstream TC trajectory predictions. Crafting perturbed inputs to steer downstream outputs toward attacker-specified trajectories is a challenging problem for several reasons. First, conventional TC detection systems are opaque, non-differentiable black boxes, making standard gradient-based attacks infeasible. Second, the extreme rarity of TC events leads to a severe class imbalance problem, making it difficult to develop attack methods that produce realistic-looking cyclone paths aligned with target trajectories. To overcome these limitations, we propose Cyc-Attack, a novel method for perturbing the forecasts of DLWF models to generate adversarial trajectories. The proposed method uses a differentiable surrogate model to approximate the TC detector's output, enabling the application of gradient-based attacks. Cyc-Attack also employs a skewness-aware loss function with a kernel dilation strategy to address the severe class imbalance problem. Distance-based gradient weighting and regularization strategies are also introduced to constrain perturbations to eliminate unrealistic-looking TC paths. Our experiments show that Cyc-Attack achieves a higher true positive rate in matching the target trajectories, along with lower false alarm rates and stealthier perturbations than conventional attack methods. We further demonstrate that the adversarial upstream forecasts generated by Cyc-Attack can be leveraged as initial guidance to train an end-to-end model for learning adversarial input samples that would induce target trajectories.

♻ ☆ Generative sequence modeling for infinite memory processes via predictive states
Michael Wieck-Sosa, Cosma Rohilla Shalizi
We consider estimating the one-step-ahead conditional distribution of a multivariate stochastic process. Many existing approaches rely on assumptions such as finite-range memory, sparsity, or additivity, which can be poorly suited to processes with long-range nonlinear interactions. However, without such structural assumptions, nonparametric estimation is challenging due to the curse of dimensionality. To address this challenge, we introduce a new estimator based on learning representations of the \emph{predictive states} of a stochastic process. We show that the statistical complexity of the estimation problem is determined by the dimension of this predictive state representation. Furthermore, we show that a $p$-dimensional predictive state space can be represented in a $2p+1$-dimensional feature space. Our results imply that faster convergence rates are achievable when the predictive state space is lower-dimensional, i.e., when the past history can be compressed into a lower-dimensional statistic that is sufficient for predicting the future. We establish theoretical convergence rate guarantees for an instantiation of our method based on deep neural network estimators. We implement our method in PyTorch and evaluate its performance on synthetic data and real \emph{C. elegans} data.

☆ Combinatorial Bernoulli Factories with Polynomially Many Coins
Renato Paes Leme, Rad Niazadeh
We provide an efficient implementation of combinatorial Bernoulli factories. Such a factory turns coins of unknown biases $x$ into a random vertex of a polytope $P$ whose mean is exactly $x$. For every affine slice of the cube (the class of polytopes that admit a factory), we give a single algorithm whose expected number of coin flips and running time at every interior $x$ are polynomial in the dimension and in $1/{δ_*}$, where ${δ_*}=\min_i\{x_i,1-x_i\}$ is never supplied to the algorithm. For perfect matchings this gives $O(n^{8}{δ_*}^{-2}\log(n/{δ_*}))$ flips, while the factory of Niazadeh, Paes Leme, and Schneider [STOC 2021] spends at least $n^{2n-1}$ flips in expectation at the uniform doubly stochastic matrix. For other polytopes, our method rounds exactly given a point deep inside $P$ and the promise that $x$ is far from the boundary of $P$.
☆ GraphInfer: Statistical Inference for Decomposable Graphical Models in R
Rodrigo Labouriau
Decomposable graphical models combine closed-form maximum likelihood estimation with local model comparison, which makes structure inference practical with many variables. The R package GraphInfer provides one likelihood framework for decomposable models of continuous, discrete and mixed data, the last as conditional Gaussian models. Structure inference ranges from exact minimum forests and stepwise search to stochastic global search. Nested models are compared by likelihood-ratio tests whose null distributions are exact in finite samples: conditionally on the discrete data for edges with a continuous endpoint, and conditionally on the discrete margins of the smaller model for edges between discrete variables. Missing values are handled by EM, by structural EM, which reuses complete-data searches through a weighted pseudo-sample of expected sufficient statistics, and by multiple imputation; selected models are fit to the observed-data likelihood. The package also treats the graphical models induced by irreversible event accumulation on trees: a search over the compatible graphs whose tree moves overcome an obstruction to single-edge moves, fitting of the full accumulation model with measurement noise and bootstrap tests of the accumulation hypothesis. GraphInfer is an independent, pure R successor to the archived package gRapHD. The implementation is validated against independent references, and simulation studies inform its defaults.

☆ Sticky Manifold Piecewise Deterministic Monte Carlo for Bayesian Model Averaging
Hirofumi Shiba, Luke Hardcastle, Kengo Kamatani
Assigning positive prior probability to lower-dimensional submodels enriches the range of uncertainty that Bayesian models can represent. The resulting posterior distributions combine continuous parameter uncertainty with discrete model uncertainty. Efficient movement between these submodels, however, can be difficult to design. We propose the sticky manifold construction as a principled, modular framework for combining piecewise deterministic Markov processes (PDMPs) across different submodels. The integration is rejection-free, requires no additional likelihood evaluations, and retains the non-reversible and ballistic nature of the component PDMP dynamics. We prove that the resulting process leaves the intended mixed-dimensional target invariant. We also develop a manifold PDMP algorithm based on coordinate charts to provide the within-submodel dynamics and a blow-up procedure that resolves singular sets into codimension-one sticky boundaries. This geometric construction makes the remaining design choices explicit; component dynamics and unsticking kernels can be chosen freely, subject to easily verifiable velocity compatibility conditions. Finally, we demonstrate the sticky manifold algorithms in Bayesian model averaging examples, propagating uncertainty over pure versus mixed states in quantum state tomography, rank in Bayesian principal component analysis, and parametric families in survival extrapolation.

Building on previous work developed mainly in the GARCH framework, we derive analytical expressions for the score vector and the Hessian matrix of the Multiplicative Error Model log-likelihood by adopting the Gamma distribution for estimation purposes. Then, we illustrate how the iterative algorithm based on the analytical derivatives should be computationally implemented. After maximizing the log-likelihood, we also provide explicit formulas for several estimators of the asymptotic covariance matrix of the MLE. Additionally, we provide analytic formulas for robust covariance estimators that remain valid under distributional misspecification, which are also referred to as the asymptotic variance of the Quasi-Maximum Likelihood Estimator. We also propose a covariance estimator that is consistent under general forms of heteroskedasticity of the error term, while the usually adopted estimators rely on a specific variance assumption. The finite-sample performance of the covariance estimators is assessed through a Monte Carlo investigation. An application on real data completes the analysis.
♻ ☆ A perturbation theory for Feynman-Kac models and their particle interpretations
Pierre Del Moral, Mathieu Gerber
We develop a perturbation analysis of Feynman--Kac models, describing how local errors introduced at each step of the Feynman--Kac recursion propagate over time. Under general conditions on the potential functions and the Markov transitions, which are shown to hold for a large class of state-space models, we prove that the global error for any time horizon $T\geq 1$ is bounded by $C\,Δ_T\log(1+Δ_T^{-1})$, where $Δ_T$ is the largest local error; this bound holds both for the prediction and the updated models. These conditions require no Lyapunov function and no stability of the Markov transitions, and allow for non-compact state spaces: confinement is provided by the potential functions. Our perturbation bounds hold in total variation and in the Kolmogorov norm; for the latter, we extend the Hardy--Krause variation and the Koksma--Hlawka inequality to unbounded domains. Our perturbation theory is applied to derive time-uniform bounds for linearized Kalman filters, Euler schemes for partially observed diffusions and nudged state-space models, as well as high-probability error bounds, uniform over whole trajectories, for particle filters and, more generally, for mean field particle methods such as sequential Monte Carlo and diffusion Monte Carlo algorithms.

♻ ☆ Scentree: a framework for generating scenario trees for multistage stochastic programming
Cristian Pachón-García, Albert Solà Vilalta, F. -Javier Heredia
We present scentree, an open-source Python package for constructing scenario trees for multistage stochastic programming models using either historical data or samples drawn from a probability distribution. It combines machine learning and multivariate time series models to obtain a scenario fan that captures dependencies in the stochastic processes. This scenario fan is subsequently reduced into a scenario tree that preserves representativeness of the stochastic process, providing a flexible and extensible framework for uncertainty modeling in stochastic programming problems. The framework can also be naturally applied to two-stage stochastic programming problems. Key contributions are the joint modeling of the stochastic process, preserving correlations between all random variables, and the automation of the complete workflow, including forecasting model selection, parameter estimation, scenario fan generation, and scenario tree construction. In addition, scentree does not assume any underlying data distribution, reducing the statistical expertise required to produce a scenario tree, and is modular by design, allowing external forecasts and other partial executions of the workflow.
♻ ☆ R Package iglm: Regression under Interference in Connected Populations
Cornelius Fritz, Michael Schweinberger
We introduce R package iglm, which implements a unifying regression framework for studying relationships among binary, count-, and real-valued predictors and outcomes in connected populations with interference due to spillover, contagion, and other complex phenomena. On the computational side, the regression framework provides scalable methods that can be applied to small and large data sets, by solving a convex optimization program based on pseudo-likelihoods via accelerated Minorization-Maximization algorithms. On the statistical side, the regression framework comes with provable theoretical guarantees for statistical estimators, including consistency results and rates of convergence for maximum pseudo-likelihood estimators. To increase the versatility of iglm, users can add custom-built model terms. We showcase iglm using data on hate speech on the social media platform X and communications among students.

☆ REWEAVE: Online Learning for Workload-Adaptive HNSW Indexes
Minghao Li, Nick Koudas, Raghav Mittal
Vector databases rely on Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) indexes for similarity search, but a graph built from data alone can be poorly matched to a skewed or changing query workload. We present REWEAVE (Reward-Guided Rewiring of Vector Graphs), an online index-maintenance method that learns edge utility from query feedback and periodically rewires the bottom layer within the original per-node degree cap. The method supports sparse exact-neighbor feedback combined with self-labels, and standard HNSW serving without learning overhead once adaptation is disabled. Under explicit assumptions we prove value-estimation and graph-stabilization guarantees. Under stationary skew, REWEAVE improves held-out recall by up to 23.3 percentage points over HNSW. In comparisons with query-aware baselines on up to 100M vectors, it achieves up to 3.3x NGFix's query throughput at recall@100 of 0.80. On Amazon-ESCI with query drift, it increases stream recall@100 from 0.745 to 0.979 with 34% fewer search distance computations than frozen HNSW. These results illustrate the potential to improve retrieval quality and reduce search effort within an existing graph-degree budget, while incurring additional work during adaptation.

☆ Wayfinder: Adaptive Resource Routing from Agent Citations NeurIPS 2026
Miguel Romero, George Karypis
To act effectively, agents must gather contextual information across resources such as chats, issue trackers, email and knowledge bases, to answer questions like "what was decided in the last project meeting?" or "where is the FAQ for our internal tooling?" Where this information lives in a user's environment is unknown to the agent, so it re-explores the same resources across consecutive interactions. Common routing approaches represent each resource as a tool and rely on high-level descriptions to generalize to unseen environments. Such descriptions often fail to separate similar or overlapping resources and cannot improve from the agent's subsequent interactions. We introduce Wayfinder, an adaptive router that uses the documents cited by the downstream agent as feedback about where relevant information resides. These citations update Wayfinder's internal resource representations, which subsequent interactions use to prioritize the resources likely to contain relevant information. We also introduce resource augmentation during offline reinforcement learning, which anonymizes and permutes resource identities to discourage training-time overfitting of which resource holds which topic; our ablations suggest it helps most when few training environments are available. Because no openly available professional environments pair realistic queries with resource-access patterns, we construct and release three controlled testbeds derived from existing datasets: NFCorpus, FEVER and Tech Startup. Compared with supervised, tool-retrieval and contextual bandit baselines under a shared closed-loop protocol, Wayfinder gives the best routing when resources contain semantically overlapping content that static descriptions cannot distinguish, while description-based tool retrieval suffices when resources are drawn from distinct corpora.

☆ Predicting the Needle in a Petabyte Scale Haystack: Open-Vocabulary Event Anticipation in Satellite Imagery NeurIPS 2026
Shreelekha Revankar, Mikhail Klassen, Creon Levit, Ash Hoover, Kavita Bala, Bharath Hariharan
Satellite constellations now image the Earth daily, capturing the lifecycle of events from deforestation to urban construction. Anticipating these events before completion enables timely intervention, yet existing systems cannot jointly identify where a change occurs, what it will become, and when it will finish across an open vocabulary. Building such a model requires diverse event data, but events are like needles in a haystack, making manual annotation at global scale infeasible. We address this problem by representing change as the vector difference between vision-language model embeddings at distinct time points. This arithmetic approach allows us to search for semantic transformations directly in the latent space, enabling (1) an automated data engine for global event discovery without manual annotation and (2) the largest global satellite event dataset to our knowledge, comprising 21,000+ locations across 64+ event types with ~2M images from PlanetScope and Sentinel-2 spanning six continents, to train (3) a novel global-scale event anticipation model. Our model detects change with a 93.5% max F1 score, outperforms baselines 3.6x on predicted event retrieval, and forecasts completion dates with a 3-day median error, even nine months before completion. Code: https://github.com/ShreelekhaR/predicting-the-needle

Lingxiao Kong, Vasileios Arampatzakis, Vasileios Sevetlidis, George Pavlidis, Zeyd Boukhers
Cultural heritage sites are increasingly monitored by sensor networks, but querying their data requires database expertise. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a natural-language interface, yet over raw sensor records they lose track of which sensor, site, and time each value belongs to, and silently miscompute. On 500 questions over real data from five heritage sites, HeriKGQA reaches 99.0% accuracy, 18.2 points above the strongest of three baselines using the same LLM and receiving the same anomaly rules and answer conventions, with comparable answer quality while running almost four times faster. Without grounding, accuracy drops by 12.2 points and on anomaly questions from 99% to 66%. We report lessons from development and live deployment.

☆ When Local Definitions Are Missing: Stable Errors in Language Models
Zengqing Wu, Chuan Xiao
Contracts, technical manuals, and online communities often give familiar words special meanings and define them in one place. A language model that reads a passage without that definition may use the usual meaning and give an answer that sounds right but is wrong. We study this with multiple-choice questions whose correct answers depend on a local definition. The questions come from a synthetic vocabulary, commercial contracts, Reddit community glossaries, and the documentation of a decentralized exchange. We ask three language models each question with and without the definition. Without using the answer key, we then test whether their repeated answers and stated confidence reveal their own errors. Separately, we give a small open model the answer key and test whether it can predict which questions larger models get wrong. We report three findings. (1) Familiar words that a source redefines cause the most errors. Models often repeat the same wrong answer, and neither repeated answers nor stated confidence reliably flag it. (2) The source definition fixes most errors on synthetic questions, but a definition drawn from the model's own prior knowledge does not. In real contracts, the source definition fixes only about half of the errors. (3) Given an answer key, a small model can rank questions by how likely larger models are to get them wrong. These results call for tests that check answers against the full source, including its local definitions.

Re-ranking refines the upstream ranked list to maximize listwise user utility. The generator is trained in two stages: supervised pre-training on logged exposure lists to establish a relevance prior, followed by reward-guided post-training that aligns the generator with the reward model through complementary distribution and ranking alignment over within-pool standardized rewards. Extensive offline experiments show that ReAlign consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines.

An exact margin decomposition shows that both directions are correct only when the direction-sensitive query--document interaction exceeds the direction-invariant pair preference. Empirically, direction-sensitive changes are common, but their aligned interaction is usually too weak to overcome that preference. Diagnostic fine-tuning shows that models can learn relational behavior that generalizes across relation families, with stronger generalization in the larger model.

Furthermore, we conduct a large-scale online controlled experiment at a major video-streaming platform in Asia, where we show that our method significantly increases click-through rate, video views, and time spent over the latest production system, leading to tangible economic impact for the company. Our method has since been deployed on the platform and remains in operation. Our findings establish consumer curiosity as a measurable and actionable objective for recommender systems, with important managerial implications for digital platforms to recommend what consumers wonder about.

CTR is not specific to HNSW, and we also evaluate it on another graph index.

♻ ☆ When Does Low-Bit Quantization Preserve the Decisions of Vector Search?
Wenxuan Xiao, Xu Cao
An orthogonal rotation improves the distance rank correlation of two-bit Cohere codes from 0.75 to 0.91, yet increases nearest-neighbour comparison flips by 51%. We analyse quantization through the comparisons made by graph search. A comparison changes only when its quantization error exceeds its exact margin, giving a flip bound that separates close calls from large errors. Shared endpoints induce correlated distance errors that partly cancel within a comparison. An exact replay identity connects candidate-level actions to the output of neighbour selection. A Gaussian model gives coordinate-code errors in closed form, and a rare-spike construction exposes heavy tails in the population-radius error. Held-out blocks give model-free certificates for acceptance rules based on exact or quantized margins. Across 24 dataset-code configurations, calibration-estimated risk correlates with held-out ranking and pruning flips at 0.97 and 0.99, compared with 0.91 and 0.99 for a margin-to-noise summary and 0.74 and 0.05 for distance rank correlation. Paired builds of 200,000-vector graphs connect rotation, query scoring, and topology to end-to-end recall and search work.
comment: 51 pages, 5 figures; substantially revised with expanded theory, calibration controls, and graph-search experiments
♻ ☆ The Oracle and The Prism: A Decoupled and Efficient Framework for Generative Recommendation Explanation
Jiaheng Zhang, Daqiang Zhang
The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into explainable recommendation systems often leads to a performance-efficiency trade-off in end-to-end architectures, where joint optimization of ranking and explanation can result in suboptimal compromises. To resolve this, we propose Prism, a novel decoupled framework that rigorously separates the recommendation process into a dedicated ranking stage and an explanation generation stage. This decomposition ensures that each component is optimized for its specific objective, eliminating inherent conflicts in coupled models. Inspired by knowledge distillation, Prism leverages a powerful, instruction-following teacher LLM (FLAN-T5-XXL) as an Oracle to produce high-fidelity explanatory knowledge. A compact, fine-tuned student model (BART-Base), the Prism, then specializes in synthesizing this knowledge into personalized explanations. Our extensive experiments on benchmark datasets reveal a key finding: the distillation process not only transfers knowledge but also acts as a noise filter. Our 140M-parameter Prism model significantly outperforms its 11B-parameter teacher in human evaluations of faithfulness and personalization, demonstrating an emergent ability to correct hallucinations present in the teacher's outputs. While achieving a 24x speedup and a 10x reduction in memory consumption, our analysis validates that decoupling, coupled with targeted distillation, provides an efficient and effective pathway to high-quality, and perhaps more importantly, trustworthy explainable recommendation.

♻ ☆ Toward Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Enterprise Retail Workflows over Heterogeneous Data Sources KDD 2027
Jeonghwan Choi, Jibin Hwang, Hayoon Park, Hyeonjae Cheon, Hwanjun Song
Enterprise retail workflows require agents to chain evidence across heterogeneous sources, from structured product and order records to unstructured inquiries and reviews, yet existing agentic RAG benchmarks rarely capture this challenge. To enable controlled evaluation of such workflows, we introduce RetailBridge, a compositional retail benchmark built from persona-driven simulations. Its questions are constructed by linking entities and intermediate answers across heterogeneous sources, requiring agents to identify the relevant sources, carry evidence between them, and produce a grounded answer. To systematically evaluate LLMs on these retail workflows, we develop RetailRAG, a retail-aware framework equipped with auto-schema briefing, source-routed plan chaining, and diagnostic plan revision. RetailRAG consistently outperforms existing agentic RAG baselines across all evaluation axes, serving as a strong reference system for assessing LLM agents on retail workflows. On RetailBridge, evaluating ten LLM backbones with RetailRAG reveals multi-source chaining as the dominant bottleneck across providers and model scales, suggesting that reliable retail agents require explicit cross-source orchestration rather than scaling alone. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/DISL-Lab/RetailBridge.

♻ ☆ What Score Distillation Transfers to Compact Dense Retrievers
Kirill Dubovikov, Martin Takac, Salem Lahlou
Compact retrievers are often specialized by distilling a large embedding model's similarity scores on hard negatives mined by the teacher model. We argue that this common setup calls for a different loss than the scale-dependent ones usually used, such as MarginMSE and PairMSE. When the teacher discards candidates scored too close to the labeled positive, the negatives it keeps get nearly identical scores. These losses then mostly ask the student to reproduce this tiny score range rather than the teacher's ranking. A per-row Pearson correlation loss, invariant to the shift and scale of the scores in each row (a query and its 32 candidates), avoids this failure, and removing PairMSE's scale term alone recovers most of Pearson's lead. We propose row scale dispersion, computed from the untrained student before training, to tell when this matters. With this loss, on rows mined around a labeled document, the teacher's scores substitute for relevance labels rather than add to them. Training on the binary label alone works as well, with the same loss or, for one student, a contrastive loss: the teacher's value lies in choosing the negatives. Without labels, the teacher's scores on its own top-ranked documents recover most of the labeled gain, largely through its top document as a pseudo-label. Experiments with two compact students on three BEIR datasets support both conclusions, including, for one student, comparisons with MarginMSE and a tuned listwise KL. We suggest a simple practical rule: distill teacher-mined negatives with a scale-free loss and, on such rows, use the teacher's scores where labels are missing rather than on top of them.

☆ A Matching Lower Bound for Online Smooth Calibration
Kaixuan Ji, Quanquan Gu
We study smooth calibration error in sequential binary prediction, which measures how far a sequence of probabilistic forecasts is from being calibrated and, unlike the classical expected calibration error, is robust to small perturbations of the forecasts. Against adaptive adversaries, the minimax smooth calibration error is known to lie between $Ω(T^{1/3})$ and $O(\sqrt{T})$ (Qiao and Zheng, 2024), where $T$ is the number of rounds. In this paper, we close this gap by constructing a new adversary whose outcome mean moves with the forecaster's cumulative residual. This design makes compensating for past residuals costly, and forces every forecaster to incur an expected smooth calibration error of $Ω(\sqrt{T})$. This lower bound matches the known upper bound up to universal constants, and further implies $Ω(\sqrt{T})$ lower bounds for calibration distance and lower calibration distance. Overall, our results settle the minimax rates of these calibration measures in sequential prediction. The proof ideas are partially developed by GPT-6 Astra under the authors' guidance.
☆ Your PID Is Already a Neural Network: Learning Its Gains with Only Three Weights and No Teacher
Felipe de Jesús Félix-Arredondo, Nezih Nieto-Gutiérrez, Carlos Astengo-Noguez, Alejandro Ucan-Puc
A discrete PID controller is exactly a recurrent neural network, a classical state-space fact: a fixed linear memory of the running integral and the last error, read out by three trainable weights that map one-to-one to the PID gains. Networks with bounded hidden states, such as LSTMs of any width, only approximate it. Trained only on a one-step physical cost (the expected cost of one transition from a fixed state distribution), with no demonstrations, teacher controller, or known gains, the network solves a strongly convex least-squares problem, so gradient descent converges from any initialization to the unique one-step optimal PID gains; the limit network is that PID, with the same action on every error sequence. Partitioned regression then shows what extra capacity buys. Orthogonal residual features keep these gains and improve on the PID if and only if they correlate with the part of the optimal action outside the PID span. On a nonlinear second-order example the gap is 5.88% of the optimal PID cost, and 4.00% against PID with a bias; no controller can improve on PID by more on this objective. A residual started at a tuned PID begins exactly at that PID; at the one-step optimal PID, a fixed-feature residual's first gradient step lowers the cost if and only if its features can improve on the PID. Experiments confirm the realization, recovery, and gap results to numerical precision. On held-out plants of three families, under a protocol frozen before the test data existed, a residual warm-started at a heavily tuned PID and trained with it lowers the long-horizon cost by 3.5%, 3.5%, and 1.9%, with family-wise 95% bounds excluding zero, also under distribution shift; a post hoc comparison with the PID tuned alone suggests that most of it comes from the recurrent part in two families. The primary endpoint, a gain of at least 5% from a generic PID start, is not met in any family.

☆ Improved Elastic Weight Consolidation as an Optimization Constraint for Continual Learning
Davide Wiest
Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) is a widely used regularization-based technique for continual learning, protecting performance on old tasks with a quadratic penalty whose empirical Fisher is usually justified through probabilistic curvature. We instead introduce Continual Learning as an Optimization Constraint (CLOC): new training must preserve chosen functionals of learned behavior. EWC's empirical Fisher is exactly the first-order form of this constraint when the preserved functional is each sample's loss. This derivation exposes a flaw: EWC implicitly weights each sample by the scale of its loss gradient, so well-fitted samples lose importance. EWC-DR observed this failure in classification; CLOC identifies its general cause. Improved Elastic Weight Consolidation (IEWC) penalizes output changes according to the first-order approximation of each old sample's loss level set, removing the weighting for any differentiable loss and output geometry, and prevents corrupt samples from dominating the importance matrix. Across classification, segmentation, language, forecasting, and diffusion, IEWC variants match or improve on EWC and outperform EWC-DR. In a held-out evaluation with validation-selected hyperparameters, uniform IEWC improves ImageNet-R accuracy over matched EWC by 2.00 percentage points (95% CI 0.93-3.07).

☆ Characterizing the Edge of Stability in Variational Training Without Priors NeurIPS 2026
Juraj Marusic, Jonathan Wenger, Beau Coker, John P. Cunningham
Variational approaches in deep learning promise to deliver improved uncertainty quantification and out-of-distribution generalization by inferring a distribution over weights, regularized by a divergence to a chosen prior. However, prior elicitation presents a significant challenge in deep learning, resulting in the common practice of significantly downweighting the regularization term in the variational objective. Recently, it was proposed to train solely via the expected loss by relying on implicit regularization from the optimizer, rather than explicit regularization from the divergence to the prior. While this approach largely sidesteps the issue of prior elicitation, current theory lacks an understanding of how key optimization hyperparameters impact the implicit regularization. Here, we theoretically and empirically demonstrate that larger learning rates and fewer parameter samples lead to flatter minima of the loss landscape, which are known to generalize better. We show that training on the expected loss operates at a modified edge of stability, characterized by the signal-to-noise ratio of the gradient estimates and the number of Monte Carlo samples. Experiments on out-of-distribution benchmark datasets confirm the practical significance of the theoretical results.

☆ Training Calibrated Conditional Generative Models with a Sample-Only Coverage Loss
Benjamin Remy, Raphael Rossellini, Chihway Chang, Rebecca Willett
Conditional generative models have become the tool of choice for sampling posteriors in scientific inverse problems, where we seek to sample images or signals conditioned on a set of indirect and noisy measurements. Yet they are often overconfident, which is a critical failure in scientific applications where accurate uncertainty quantification is essential. Existing regularizers fall short in complementary ways: differentiable coverage objectives require the model's density and do not identify the posterior, while strictly proper scoring rules such as the energy score need only samples but do not directly enforce coverage. We close this gap by introducing a differentiable loss function based on the expected coverage probability, estimated from samples alone. It applies to any conditional generative model, with no need for tractable densities or architectural changes. We prove that it is a strict divergence, vanishing if and only if the model equals the true posterior. On simulation-based inference benchmarks, it matches a density-based coverage loss without evaluating the density. On high-dimensional imaging inverse problems, it yields better-calibrated posteriors than scoring-rule regularizers, with little change in the reconstruction quality of point estimates.

♻ ☆ There Will Be a Scientific Theory of Deep Learning
Jamie Simon, Daniel Kunin, Alexander Atanasov, Enric Boix-Adserà, Blake Bordelon, Jeremy Cohen, Nikhil Ghosh, Florentin Guth, Arthur Jacot, Mason Kamb, Dhruva Karkada, Eric J. Michaud, Berkan Ottlik, Joseph Turnbull
In this paper, we make the case that a scientific theory of deep learning is emerging. By this we mean a theory which characterizes important properties and statistics of the training process, hidden representations, final weights, and performance of neural networks. We pull together major strands of ongoing research in deep learning theory and identify five growing bodies of work that point toward such a theory: (a) solvable idealized settings that provide intuition for learning dynamics in realistic systems; (b) tractable limits that reveal insights into fundamental learning phenomena; (c) simple mathematical laws that capture important macroscopic observables; (d) theories of hyperparameters that disentangle them from the rest of the training process, leaving simpler systems behind; and (e) universal behaviors shared across systems and settings which clarify which phenomena call for explanation. Taken together, these bodies of work share certain broad traits: they are concerned with the dynamics of the training process; they primarily seek to describe coarse aggregate statistics; and they emphasize falsifiable quantitative predictions. We argue that the emerging theory is best thought of as a mechanics of the learning process, and suggest the name learning mechanics. We discuss the relationship between this mechanics perspective and other approaches for building a theory of deep learning, including the statistical and information-theoretic perspectives. In particular, we anticipate a symbiotic relationship between learning mechanics and mechanistic interpretability. We also review and address common arguments that fundamental theory will not be possible or is not important. We conclude with a portrait of important open directions in learning mechanics and advice for beginners. We host further introductory materials, perspectives, and open questions at learningmechanics.pub.

♻ ☆ Conflict Forecasting via Conformal Prediction for Markov Processes
Aditya Basarkar, Emmett B. Kendall, David Randahl, Jonathan P. Williams, Gudmund H. Hermansen
Whether or not a country is at war, or experiencing escalating or deescalating levels of conflict, has massive ramifications on a country's national and foreign policy. Given a country's history of conflict, or lack thereof, future predictions about the war-status of a country are valuable information. In this paper, we present the use of conformal prediction on temporally-dependent data to obtain prediction sets of possible future conflict state-sequences. More specifically, we compare the results of conformal prediction to a likelihood-based prediction strategy when the data are assumed to come from a discrete-state Markov process. A point-prediction may not supply sufficient information because the penalty for a wrong prediction is extreme, and so we consider a machine learning alternative that gives valid uncertainty quantification and is robust to model misspecification. In the data analysis, we present real forecasts of conflict dynamics across multiple countries. Lastly, we assess the differences between the conformal and likelihood-based prediction sets applied to training data which fall under a pervasive edge-case, not discussed in existing literature.
♻ ☆ A second order regret bound for NormalHedge NeurIPS 2026
Yoav Freund, Nicholas J. A. Harvey, Victor S. Portella, Yabing Qi, Yu-Xiang Wang
We consider the problem of prediction with expert advice for "easy" sequences. We show that a variant of NormalHedge enjoys a second-order $ε$-quantile regret bound of $O(\sqrt{V_T \log(V_T/ε)})$ when $V_T > \log N$, where $V_T$ is the cumulative second moment of the instantaneous per-expert regret, averaged with respect to a natural distribution $\mathbf{q}_t$ determined by the algorithm. The algorithm is motivated by a continuous time limit using Stochastic Differential Equations. The discrete time analysis uses self-concordance techniques.

♻ ☆ Extrapolation of Periodic Functions Using Binary Encoding of Continuous Numerical Values
Brian P. Powell, Jordan A. Caraballo-Vega, Mark L. Carroll, Thomas Maxwell, Andrew Ptak, Greg Olmschenk, Jorge Martinez-Palomera
We introduce Normalized Base-2 Encoding (NB2E) as a method for encoding continuous numerical values and demonstrate that, using this input encoding, vanilla multi-layer perceptrons (MLP) successfully extrapolate four periodic waveforms without prior knowledge of their functional form. We contrast this finding with fixed Fourier encoding, which extrapolates well when the number of signal cycles over the normalized domain is an even integer and loses coherence at most other values, whereas NB2E degrades gradually away from those values and, except near odd cycle counts, remains substantially more accurate. These findings are limited to a single MLP architecture trained on one synthetic, exactly periodic, one-dimensional signal at a time, with extrapolation extending only to the end of the normalized domain. We do not propose a mechanism for this phenomenon. Rather, we present empirical observations which merit further study.
