We study the minimization of the average of $n$ convex $(L_0,L_1)$-smooth functions: the Hessian norm of each function is bounded by an affine function of its gradient norm. We assume known upper bounds $R$ on the distance from the starting point to a minimizer and $δ$ on the difference between the minimum of the average and the average of the infima of the components. We derive upper and lower bounds on the oracle complexity of reaching accuracy $\varepsilon$ in function value in expectation. Up to logarithmic factors, both bounds are of order $n(1+(L_1R)^{2/3}) +\sqrt{\frac{n(L_0+L_1^2δ)R^2}{\varepsilon}+n(L_1R)^2}$. The upper bound is attained by the proposed method YETI. The method combines ideas of accelerated proximal methods and variance reduction methods with a heuristic for choosing additional points. The number of oracle calls made by the heuristic is bounded, which preserves the upper bound on the total number of queries needed to reach the target accuracy. In the experiments, YETI is compared with first-order methods on synthetic problems and Poisson regression problems. We also examine the stopping criterion and the effect of the heuristic separately. The lower bound is obtained by an explicit construction of families of instances that are hard for any first-order method.
comment: 57 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables, 5 algorithms. Second paper in the Descending Everest series; Part I: arXiv:2610.21461
☆ Nonparametric GARCH: An Iterated Neural Estimator
Ruizhi Deng, Guohao Shen, Ngai Hang Chan
We study nonparametric estimation and forecasting for GARCH-type processes and propose an iterated neural estimator that alternates between estimating the recursion map and updating the unobserved conditional variances. Under mild conditions, we establish finite-sample bounds for the time-averaged in-sample variance-path error and show that the estimator is minimax rate-optimal up to logarithmic factors. Under stationarity and mixing conditions, we establish the same rate for recursion-map estimation and derive finite-sample bounds for out-of-sample variance forecasts and expected excess Gaussian quasi-likelihood (QLIKE) loss. The convergence rates depend on the true lag orders and remain unchanged when the fitted orders are overspecified. Simulation studies illustrate the effectiveness of our estimators under nonlinear and time-varying volatility dynamics. Real-data applications suggest that our neural methods perform competitively and can incorporate option-price and high-frequency information.
☆ Generative Modeling for Cascading Extremes via Autoregressive Transformers
Miguel de Carvalho, Myung Won Lee, Jordan Richards, Sotirios Sabanis
Extreme events often occur sequentially, from earthquake-tsunami cascades to successive extreme losses in financial markets. We introduce an extremal token representation that encodes multivariate observations as a categorical sequence. A quiet token records the absence of threshold exceedances; otherwise, the token identifies the exceeding component with the largest marginal probability-scale score. The representation is invariant to componentwise strictly increasing transformations. It preserves the identity and temporal ordering of dominant exceedances but discards their magnitudes and the identities of nondominant simultaneous exceedances. A decoder-only transformer estimates the history-dependent next-token kernel on this representation, and recursive sampling generates future token sequences from the induced joint predictive law. We amortize our generative model by pretraining across simulated process families with varying parameters and dependence persistence. Next-token predictions are evaluated against exact conditional probabilities for held-out categorical processes and particle filter references for heavy-tailed vector autoregressive processes. Applied to ten-second returns for five semiconductor stocks, the pretrained model supports zero-shot transfer, while a few epochs of adaptation improve agreement between observed and generated token frequencies and transition patterns. These results support task-specific tokenization and simulation-based pretraining for modeling which dimensions dominate multivariate extremes.
comment: 28 pages, 10 figures
☆ Balance-Guided Forest for Causal Effect Estimation
Feiyang Yi, Jelena Bradic
Covariate balancing is widely used for estimating causal effects in observational studies. A central challenge is determining which covariate features should be balanced. Forest-kernel balancing provides a data-driven way to learn informative balancing features. Existing forest-kernel balancing methods first learn a tree-based representation and then construct balancing weights. However, this procedure creates a mismatch, as limited tree capacity may be spent on features that are already well represented. We propose Balance-Guided Forest (BGF), which uses the current balancing weights to guide subsequent tree construction. BGF grows trees using a novel splitting score that combines residual imbalance with an outcome contrast, favoring splits that separate outcome-relevant regions where imbalance remains. This couples representation learning with covariate balancing rather than treating balancing as a downstream step. We establish an oracle-type bound that links the iterative construction to weighting error and causal bias. Simulations exhibit improvements in causal estimation relative to existing forest-kernel approaches. Real-data applications illustrate the practical behavior of BGF across observational studies.
☆ From Type to Token: Petri Nets, Individual Token Philosophy, and Individualized Causal Effects
Fernando Delbianco, Fernando Tohmé, Gustavo Bodanza
Structural Causal Models and Bayesian Networks are the dominant framework for representing causal relations. They are fundamentally type-level formalisms since their estimands, Average Treatment Effects and Conditional Average Treatment Effects, are properties of distributions over populations, not of individual units. When treatment effects exhibit unbounded heterogeneity, these estimands collapse. What persists is the structural, token-level core of causation. We argue that Petri Nets under the Individual Token Philosophy are the natural representation of these token-level causal structures. We develop a formal translation from Bayesian Networks to Petri Nets, providing a two-layer account of individualized causality. The PN layer provides a structural representation of causal mechanisms that does not rest on distributional assumptions. In turn, a conformal prediction layer quantifies causal effects with finite-sample coverage guarantees. Together they constitute a complete account of individual causal effects.

Matthew S. Scott, Yaniv Plan, Özgür Yılmaz
We show exact signal recovery in generative compressed sensing for feedforward neural networks with piecewise-linear activations and a final sigmoid activation, with no assumption of expansivity. Consider a ReLU network of depth $d$ with a sigmoid final activation, whose input layer, of dimension $k$, is the narrowest, and let $K$ be the geometric mean of the widths of its layers. We show that, with high probability, all signals of the range whose entries lie in $[δ, 1 - δ]$ are uniformly recovered from $m \gtrsim k(d \log(K/k) + \log(1+\log(1/δ)))$ measurements.

♻ ☆ TOPPO: Rethinking PPO for Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning with Critic Balancing NeurIPS 2026
Yuanpeng Li, Gefei Lin, Annie Qu, Rui Miao
Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) and its variants dominate Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning (MTRL) due to their off-policy sample efficiency, while on-policy methods such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) remain underexplored. We diagnose that PPO in MTRL suffers from a previously overlooked issue: critic-side gradient ill-conditioning, which may cause tail tasks to stall while easy tasks dominate the value function's updates. To address this, we propose TOPPO (Tail-Optimized PPO), a reformulation of PPO via Critic Balancing -- a set of modules that improve gradient conditioning and balance learning dynamics across tasks. Unlike prior approaches that rely on modular architectures or large models, TOPPO targets the optimization bottleneck within PPO itself. Empirically, on the Meta-World+ MT50 benchmark, TOPPO achieves stronger mean and tail-task performance than prior SAC-family and ARS-family methods while using substantially fewer parameters and reaching their final performance in fewer environment steps. Notably, TOPPO matches or surpasses strong SAC baselines early in training and maintains superior performance at full budget. Ablations confirm the effectiveness of each module in TOPPO and provide insights into their interactions. Our results demonstrate that, with proper optimization, on-policy methods can rival or exceed off-policy approaches in MTRL, challenging the prevailing reliance on SAC and highlighting critic-side gradient conditioning as the central bottleneck.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Camera-ready version. 54 pages (10 main), 29 figures, 24 tables. Code: https://github.com/NAIVlab/TOPPO
♻ ☆ Quantification of Tail-trimming Effects for Interval CVaR Based Nonlinear Regression
Yulei You, Junyi Liu
The tail trimming strategy is widely adopted for robustness against outlier contamination in statistical learning and operations research. However, it generally lacks the thorough understanding that to what extent the tail-trimming technique is effective for nonlinear regression. In this paper, we address the robust nonlinear regression based on the so-called interval conditional value-at-risk (In-CVaR), which is introduced to guard against outliers by trimming extreme losses. We first analyze the trimming effect of the In-CVaR based estimator under distributional perturbation. Our first finding is that the In-CVaR based estimator is qualitatively robust under distributional perturbation in terms of the Prokhorov metric if and only if the largest portion of losses is trimmed. Furthermore, under sample contamination, we derive a probably approximately correct (PAC) bound for the In-CVaR based estimator, showing that the preliminary covariate filtering that is customary in the literature is not needed for In-CVaR based regression. The nonconvexity of the In-CVaR objective, together with unboundedness of covariates, responses and parameter space create the technical challenges for our developed theory, and thus necessitate the new treatment of the qualitative robustness and PAC analysis. Overall, this study rigorously analyzes robustness properties of In-CVaR based nonlinear regression models, which illustrates to what extent the right tail-trimming of the loss by In-CVaR risk measure is essential and effective for robust nonlinear regression. These theoretical findings are further supported by numerical experiments.
♻ ☆ Almost Sure Convergence Rates of Stochastic Approximation and Reinforcement Learning via a Poisson-Moreau Drift
Xinyu Liu, Zixuan Xie, Shangtong Zhang
Establishing almost sure convergence rates for stochastic approximation and reinforcement learning under Markovian noise is a fundamental theoretical challenge. We make progress towards this challenge for a class of stochastic approximation algorithms whose expected updates are contractive, a setting that arises in many reinforcement learning algorithms such as $Q$-learning and linear temporal difference learning. Specifically, for a power-law learning rate $O(n^{-η})$ with $η\in (1/2, 1)$, we obtain an almost sure convergence rate arbitrarily close to $o(n^{1 - 2η})$. For the harmonic learning rate $α_n=α/(n+1)$, the almost sure squared-error rate is $o(n^{-ζ})$ for every $ζ<\min\{1,2(1-κ)α\}$, where $κ$ is the contraction factor. Thus exponents arbitrarily close to one are available when $2(1-κ)α\geq1$. This approaches the $n^{-1}$ polynomial exponent of classical law-of-the-iterated-logarithm benchmarks. Key to our analysis is a novel Lyapunov drift construction that applies a Poisson-equation based correction for Markovian noise to the well-established Moreau-envelope smoothing for the contractive mapping.

Adam R. Klivans, Konstantinos Stavropoulos, Sergei Tikhonov, Arsen Vasilyan
In an important recent work, Blanc (2026) gave an algorithm for robustly learning Boolean concept classes with respect to a fixed distribution that outputs a (randomized) classifier achieving the optimal error of $η+ \varepsilon$ where $η$ is the noise rate. In contrast, it is well known that deterministic hypotheses cannot achieve error less than $2η+ \varepsilon.$ Blanc's algorithm is computationally inefficient, and the main problem left open in his work is to find a polynomial-time algorithm given access to an oracle for empirical risk minimization (ERM). In this paper, we resolve this problem and give such an algorithm. Perhaps surprisingly, our techniques make crucial use of various types of no-regret learners. Additionally, we give an efficient algorithm (no ERM oracle required) for robustly learning any function class that admits sandwiching polynomials with respect to hypercontractive distributions. As one consequence, we give the first polynomial-time algorithm for robustly learning a halfspace with respect to Gaussian marginals that achieves error $η+ \varepsilon$ for any constant $\varepsilon$.
comment: Added results on L2 polynomial approximators
♻ ☆ Score-Based Modeling of Effective Langevin Dynamics with State-Dependent Mobility
Ludovico T. Giorgini
In a previous work [L. T. Giorgini, Phys. Rev. E 114, L012102 (2026)], we introduced stochastic reduced-order models that reproduce by construction the stationary density and short-time correlations of the observed variables, using a constant mobility matrix and the score, the gradient of the logarithm of this density. Here we generalize the framework to state-dependent mobilities, calibrated so that the model also reproduces the finite-lag correlation functions of chosen target observables. The calibration uses exact finite-lag forms of the generalized fluctuation-dissipation theorem, which express time derivatives of lagged correlations as averages over observed pairs of states and are linear in the mobility. When the mobility is expanded on a basis of known fields, its coefficients follow from a least-squares problem involving only the stationary score, and the observables and basis are selected by data-driven diagnostics. Otherwise, a neural-network mobility is calibrated through the conditional score of the finite-time transition density. We validate the approach analytically on a Cox-Ingersoll-Ross process and numerically on a two-dimensional nonequilibrium diffusion with multiplicative noise and a 36-dimensional soft-spin Landau-Lifshitz chain. Both methods reproduce the stationary statistics and the target correlations accurately. Because the identities can be integrated between consecutive lags, so that no time derivatives need to be estimated, the recovered drift and diffusion are much less sensitive to coarse sampling than Kramers-Moyal estimates, which require short sampling intervals. Calibration requires no simulation of the model and applies to high-dimensional systems.
comment: 46 pages, 10 figures; revised version. Code: https://github.com/ludogiorgi/StateDependentMobility.jl (v2-revised-submission)
♻ ☆ Surprisal-Rényi Free Energy
Shion Matsumoto, Ankur Arjun Mali
The forward and reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergences arise as limiting objectives in learning and inference, yet they induce markedly different inductive biases that cannot be explained by expectation terms alone. We introduce the Surprisal-Rényi Free Energy (SRFE), a normalized Rényi-Chernoff log-moment functional of the likelihood ratio. Although SRFE is algebraically related to Rényi divergence for fixed values of the order parameter, its endpoint-symmetric normalization yields a distinct free-energy viewpoint for analyzing how forward- and reverse KL behavior emerges near singular limits. We show that SRFE recovers the forward and reverse KL divergences as endpoint limits and derive local expansions around both regimes in which the variance of the log-likelihood ratio appears as a first-order correction away from the KL objective. These expansions reveal an explicit mean-variance tradeoff governing departures from KL-dominated behavior. We further establish a Gibbs-type variational characterization in terms of weighted KL projections and prove that SRFE controls large deviations of excess code length through Chernoff-type bounds, giving a Minimum Description Length interpretation of the functional. We evaluate SRFE on two synthetic settings (two-dimensional Gaussian-mixture variational inference and multi-class classification) and the long-tailed CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (CIFAR-LT) datasets. On CIFAR-LT, retraining the best configuration of each loss over five seeds, SRFE matches cross-entropy accuracy on CIFAR-10-LT and gives mixed results on CIFAR-100-LT, improving few-shot accuracy at one of three imbalance factors. Together, these results position SRFE as a variance- and tail-sensitive, normalized Rényi-Chernoff free energy that clarifies the geometric, statistical, and large-deviation structure underlying the transition between forward- and reverse-KL limits.
♻ ☆ On Global Joint Lower Bounds in Zeroth-Order Nonconvex Optimization
Yuxuan Xia, Xiao-Tong Yuan
Must the dimension and accuracy costs of zeroth-order optimization multiply? Global upper bounds for smooth stochastic nonconvex optimization scale as $O(dε^{-4})$, with both factors separately necessary. We show that their product is unavoidable. We establish an $Ω(dε^{-4})$ lower bound for smooth stochastic nonconvex optimization, yielding an $Ω(dδ^{-1}ε^{-3})$ bound for nonsmooth Goldstein stationarity. Both match the best-known full-space upper bounds, establishing joint minimax optimality in dimension and accuracy. These bounds hold against fully adaptive randomized algorithms with unrestricted queries and outputs, even under arbitrary sample reuse. As a byproduct, we establish noiseless exact-value lower bounds for both smooth and Goldstein stationarity, even against randomized algorithms.
♻ ☆ The Price of Scale in Proactive Memory Recall
Yichuan Chen, Xin Wang
A long-lived assistant that brings up memories without being asked must decide at every turn whether anything in its store is worth an interruption. We show that this decision is a multiple-testing problem whose difficulty grows with the store size N. On replays of LongMemEval, a similarity threshold tuned to 5% false alarms at N=8 reaches 84-100% at N=2048 across embedding models and cue types; LoCoMo and LLM judges show it too. We prove that a gate which thresholds the best of N independent irrelevant scores at false-alarm rate alpha operates at a per-item false-positive rate of about -ln(1-alpha)/N, which pins its hit rate to the far left of the ROC and makes it regularly varying in N under regular variation. Replayed hit rates stay within its bounds for mixed cues up to 0.3 points, and hit rates carry over to held-out questions to within 6.0 points. At matched false alarms the deployed score recalls 14-26 points more than raw cosine. A cue-swap conformal gate, which ranks the current cue among other cues on the same store, has a finite-sample false-alarm guarantee under exchangeability. With a background from the user's unfiltered history it keeps false alarms at 3-6% on LongMemEval at the hit rate of a label-tuned threshold; on LoCoMo it overshoots or turns conservative depending on the source of its reference cues. In a chronological replay with the user's own earlier messages as references, it fires on 5-8% of questions on stores without their answer and on 6-8% of session-opening turns, against 57% for the deployed gate at N=2048, at a median 0.4 s CPU per decision. A cross-encoder pays the same price of scale, and on a prospective-memory benchmark, similarity gates recall at most 9% of constraints at controlled false alarms. One human and two LLM annotators judge most false alarms unhelpful for a response. Code and data: https://github.com/RiverChenStillCompiling/price-of-scale

♻ ☆ Deep Learning of Compositional Targets with Hierarchical Spectral Methods ICML 2026
Hugo Tabanelli, Yatin Dandi, Luca Pesce, Florent Krzakala
Why depth yields a computational advantage over shallow methods remains a central open question in learning theory. We study this question in a controlled high-dimensional Gaussian setting, focusing on compositional target functions. We analyze their learnability using an explicit three-layer fitting model trained via layer-wise spectral estimators. The target combines polynomial latent features with a scalar readout, and its compositional structure allows learning to proceed in stages. Recovering an intermediate representation reduces the problem to lower-degree spectral estimation tasks, as in multi-index models. Our analysis establishes Gaussian comparison bounds for projected moments when $0<\varepsilon<1/3$, and motivates separations in sample complexity between two- and three-layer learning strategies, conditional on a conjectured spectral recovery step.
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026. Revised version
♻ ☆ How Deep Are Deep GPs, Really? A Sharp Threshold and a Non-Gaussian Limit for Compositional GPs NeurIPS 2026
Mark Kozdoba, Shie Mannor
Compositional priors describe the generic properties of layered functions in deep Bayesian models, where deep neural networks with random weights are a canonical example. In the wide-network limit, the prior is a Gaussian process (GP) with a depth-dependent kernel, and its behaviour as depth grows has been extensively studied through this kernel. Here, we study another case, where each layer itself is a vector valued Gaussian process, and our aim is similarly to understand the limiting behaviour of the prior as depth grows. Previous GP work has established that for the radial basis function (RBF) kernel and a certain range of bandwidths $r$, the prior degenerates in the limit, converging to the set of constant functions, which is not useful as a probabilistic model. In this paper we establish several new results. First, we identify a sharp bandwidth threshold $r_c(d) = Θ(\sqrt{d})$ above which the limit is degenerate, strengthening the earlier bounds. Second, and more importantly, we show that for $r$ below the threshold $r_c(d)$ the prior converges to a limit distribution $π_{\bar{Z}}$. We also prove that these distributions are non-degenerate and non-Gaussian, with non-vanishing dependence between coordinates. In contrast to the previously known degenerate regime, deep Gaussian process priors can therefore admit non-trivial limits. Empirically, we verify the threshold across a range of dimensions $d$, and demonstrate a complex multimodal behaviour of the limit distributions $π_{\bar{Z}}$, a regime that becomes increasingly narrow with $d$ and would be hard to identify without knowing the threshold.

♻ ☆ Near Minimax Rates for Quantile Distributional Reinforcement Learning
Zijie Cheng, Zhihua Zhang
In this paper, we study quantile distributional policy evaluation, where the return distribution under a given policy is approximated by the quantile Bellman fixed point $\bmη_m$. We investigate the statistical accuracy of estimating $\bmη_m$ across quantile resolutions under Wasserstein distances. Assuming access to a generative model, we construct a quantile fixed point estimator $\bmη_m^{(n)}$ from an empirical Markov decision process of $n$ observations per state-action pair and establish non-asymptotic error bounds under Wasserstein distances. When reward densities are uniformly bounded away from zero, we obtain a root-$n$ high-probability bound simultaneously over all resolutions $m$ and all Wasserstein orders $1\le p\le\infty$. When reward densities vanish at the support endpoints, we show that continuity and endpoint monotonicity suffice to preserve the same resolution-independent rate for $1\le p\le2$. For $p>2$, we establish a root-$n$ bound with coefficient $m^{1/2-1/p}$, together with a slower, resolution-independent $n^{-1/p}$ bound for every finite $p>2$. We further obtain resolution-independent $W_\infty$ consistency governed by the continuity modulus of reward quantile functions. To investigate the sharpness of these bounds, we characterize the exact local asymptotic minimax risk at each fixed resolution as the expected Wasserstein-coordinate norm of the efficient Gaussian limit and prove that our estimator attains it. We then examine the resolution dependence of this optimal local risk. A regular one-state instance has resolution-independent local risk constants, whereas a single endpoint-vanishing two-state instance exhibits growth of order $m^{1/2-1/p}$, up to logarithmic factors along a resolution subsequence, for every $p>2$.

We study this connection in large-alphabet prediction through the *layered simplex architecture* (LSA), which multiplies independent uniform simplex vectors coordinate-wise and normalizes. At depth zero, the prior is concentrated on the uniform distribution; at depth one, the Bayesian predictor is Laplace's rule. Each additional layer shifts prior mass toward more concentrated distributions. We derive exact Bayesian marginal likelihood and regret expressions using reusable depth-specific kernels. Mixing over depths up to a cutoff logarithmic in alphabet size yields an explicit predictor with rigorous guarantees. For targets uniform on a specified sparse support, the mixture's prior complexity is asymptotic to the support-description cost at every fixed positive KL resolution, establishing a broad complexity spectrum. We also prove a regret lower bound for every label-invariant predictor: the expected description length of the discovered symbol set minus the source's uncertainty about its identity given its size. For Zipf sources in a growing-alphabet regime, the depth mixture attains this bound to leading order. Thus, the symbol-discovery rate determines the regret exponent. Although introduced to study depth, the LSA predictor competes with established large-alphabet methods, including Good--Turing, Ristad's law and an adaptive Dirichlet mixture, while substantially outperforming classical add-constant rules on concentrated sources.

SCALLOP significantly reduces both training variance and training time while consistently improving performance compared to F2D2, and is competitive with the state-of-the-art while achieving up to 10x inference speedup over the fastest baseline.

By fixing the weights of the hidden layers and training only the output layer, RaNNDy achieves significant reductions in computational costs -- often by two orders of magnitude -- with similar accuracy compared to state-of-the-art deep learning methods. The method is less sensitive to hyperparameter tuning and provides a closed-form solution for the output layer weights that directly represent eigenfunctions of the learned operator. Moreover, it is possible to estimate uncertainties associated with the computed spectral properties via ensemble learning. We demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach using diverse benchmark problems, including stochastic dynamical systems and protein folding processes, highlighting the strengths but also weaknesses of RaNNDy.

We further prove an equivalence between sinks and hard attention switch, in which the output of the attention is identically 0. Finally, we relax the hard attention switch by allowing token self-communication: we provide a quantitative comparison of the costs of representing sinks vs.\ diagonal patterns, showing why sinks are favored in pretrained transformers. We study this phenomenon in analytically tractable settings with exact score functions, characterizing its dependence on data dimensionality and the number of classes. For high-dimensional Gaussian mixtures, we use dynamic mean-field theory to show that distortions persist when the number of classes scales exponentially with the data dimension, whereas they vanish in the sub-exponential regime due to a dynamical phase transition. Moreover we found that, in the infinite-class limit, distortions remain unavoidable regardless of dimensionality because of the increasing density of classes. Finally, we show that standard CFG schedules cannot prevent variance shrinkage, and we propose a theoretically grounded guidance schedule incorporating a negative-guidance window that improves both class separability and sample diversity in real-world latent diffusion models.

Interacting spin ensembles are promising platforms for quantum sensing, but spin-spin interactions can induce complex, nonmonotonic responses to external fields, limiting the dynamic range over which the fields can be estimated unambiguously. Here, we propose a quantum-circuit-learning-inspired method to improve the dynamic range of interacting quantum sensors using optimized global control fields. We consider an ensemble of dipole-coupled spins subjected to an inhomogeneous magnetic field generated by an electric current. By optimizing the global control fields applied during sensing, we train the expectation value of the collective magnetization to approximate a prescribed monotonic target function. We also introduce a penalty on the magnetization variance to account for measurement fluctuations. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the optimized control can substantially enlarge the dynamic range compared with sensing without control. We further investigate the trade-off between dynamic range and estimation uncertainty and show that the variance penalty can reduce the uncertainty at the expense of dynamic range. These results demonstrate that learning-assisted global control provides a promising approach to improving the performance of interacting quantum sensors.

Modeling RLVR as a Markov kernel, Jensen's inequality shows that conditional dispersion depresses pass@$k$ for $k\ge2$. Once dispersion is modeled, the conditional-mean log-odds slope is below one in every pair: RLVR improves hard prompts on average, while late-$k$ loss comes from a 2%-3% minority of base-solved prompts collapsing onto a repeated modal wrong answer and resisting prefix rescue up to 4,096 tokens. In controlled runs from one base model on 3,000 new problems, all four GRPO arms fall behind near $k\approx200$ and remain behind through $k=4096$, while SFT stays significantly ahead throughout.

♻ ☆ Optimizing the Preconditioner: A Black-box Online-to-Nonconvex Conversion with Static Regret Minimization Oracles
Haichen Hu, David Simchi-Levi
Stochastic nonconvex optimization is central to training deep networks and LLMs in modern machine learning. We give a black-box reduction from stochastic nonconvex optimization to ordinary static regret minimization in online convex optimization (OCO), addressing the open problem posed by Chen and Hazan (2024). Our reduction maintains a predictable gradient tracker, while a black-box online learner $\mathcal A$ selects a preconditioner that transforms this tracker into the update direction. Given a $β$-smooth function with initial gap at most $M$ and an unbiased gradient oracle with variance bounded by $σ^2$, we bound the expected average squared gradient norm by $O(σ\sqrt{Mβ/T}+\sqrt{Mβ}\mathrm{Reg}_T(\mathcal A)/T+\frac{Mβ}{T})$, where $\mathrm{Reg}_T(\mathcal A)$ is the static regret of $\mathcal A$ against the identity preconditioner. Thus, any OCO oracle with $O(\sqrt T)$ regret recovers the classical $O(T^{-1/2})$ convergence rate. We also prove that the additive variance term cannot be removed: every conversion making a constant number of stochastic-oracle queries per round, whose guarantee is stated through static regret against a comparator that the online learner can play, must contain an additive term of order $σ\sqrt{Mβ/T}$ for sufficiently large $T$. Moreover, for every online learner, our conversion bound is tight up to universal constants. We also extend the framework to nonsmooth nonconvex optimization, still relying only on ordinary static regret, and attain the optimal convergence rate for Goldstein-type stationarity. Finally, we conduct numerical experiments on nonconvex objectives to illustrate how the reduction exploits online-selected preconditioners while using the same stochastic-oracle budget as stochastic gradient descent.

♻ ☆ Recovering Geodesic Distances from Noisy Observations STOC 2027
Charles Fefferman, Jonathan Marty, Kevin Ren
Let $(M,d,μ)$ be a nice geodesic probability space (such as a manifold) and $X=\{x_i\}_{i\in [N]} \subset M$ a finite $μ$-i.i.d. sample. Suppose we observe noisy distance random variables $d'(x_i,x_j)$. When can the true distances be recovered to small additive error? This question has attracted interest in two disparate fields: latent-space graph models and boundary-value inverse problems. We first show that, taking $N \asymp ε^{-2d-2}|\logε|$ and using runtime $O(N^{2.5+o_d (1)})$, we can recover all distances in $X$ to additive error $O(ε|\logε|)$ with high probability, assuming $\mathbb{E} d'(x_i, x_j) = F(d(x_i,x_j))$ for an unknown, increasing bilipschitz $F$ and with the $d'(x_i,x_j)$ allowed to be arbitrarily heterogeneous in their distribution as long as they are bounded in subgaussian norm. This generalizes existing work, which required $F$ to be known and made strict assumptions on the distribution of $d'(x_i, x_j)$. Achieving this generalization required a novel ``ruler-building'' procedure to learn $F$. We extend our results to a missing data case where we randomly lose access to noisy distances. Our second result uses ideas from the first to tackle a partial observability case: $X = Y \cup Z$ with $Z$ sampled from $M$ and $Y$ sampled from an observer subset satisfying visibility conditions that model the assumptions made on the boundary in boundary-value inverse problems. In this setting, we recover all pairwise distances in $Z$ to additive error $O(ε)$ with $|Z| \asymp ε^{-2d-2}|\logε|$, $|Y| \asymp ε^{-\max\{d_ν,4\}}$ with $d_ν$ determined by the volume-growth properties of the probability measure on the observer set, and runtime $O(|Z|^3)$. This is, to our knowledge, the first quantitative guarantee for this observer/observed split under noise, which complements existing stability results for boundary data.

♻ ☆ Three Routes to One Answer: Reconciling AIPW, TMLE, and Double Machine Learning for Applied Researchers
M. Ehsan Karim
Augmented inverse probability weighting (AIPW), targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE), and double/debiased machine learning (DML) are three asymptotically equivalent routes to the same efficient influence function for the average treatment effect. We contribute a worked, shared-nuisance reconciliation on real data: what a practitioner must hold fixed for the routes and their software to agree, and when they do not. Using open data on smoking cessation and weight change (n = 1566), one Super Learner library, and folds matched within schemes, we build all three by hand, in full-sample, cross-fit, and double-cross-fit variants. A semi-synthetic benchmark with known sample-average effects on a fixed design grades interval coverage. The six doubly robust estimates span 3.32--3.39 kg over repeated splits. Single runs of our code and the tmle, AIPW, DoubleML, and tmle3 packages span 3.32--3.49 kg, compatible with fitting-scheme differences and single-split noise. Over 20 seeds, the three implementations sharing our library agree within 0.01 kg in median, although one is a TMLE. Agreement can fail: with in-sample nuisance fits on a binary mortality outcome, and under poor overlap in a job-training example. We recommend diagnosing overlap before choosing an estimator, and provide a reporting checklist and software code.

♻ ☆ The Optimal Sample Complexity of Multiclass and List Learning
Chirag Pabbaraju
While the optimal sample complexity of binary classification in terms of the VC dimension is well-established, determining the optimal sample complexity of multiclass classification had remained open. The appropriate complexity parameter for multiclass classification is the DS dimension, and despite significant efforts, a gap of $\sqrt{\text{DS}}$ had persisted between the upper and lower bounds on sample complexity. Recent work by Hanneke et al. (2026) shows a novel algebraic characterization of multiclass hypothesis classes in terms of their DS dimension. Building up on this, we show that the maximum hypergraph density of any multiclass hypothesis class is upper-bounded by its DS dimension. This proves a longstanding conjecture of Daniely and Shalev-Shwartz (2014). As a consequence, we determine the optimal dependence of the sample complexity on the DS dimension for multiclass as well as list learning.

♻ ☆ Optimal Value Inference for Reinforcement Learning
Nan Lu, Ethan Lee, Ruicheng Ao, David Simchi-Levi, Junwei Lu
We study offline inference for the optimal value in reinforcement learning under finite state and action spaces. Two new nuisances are derived as fixed points of a self-induced Bellman equation, in which we approximate the maximum Bellman operator by its softmax correspondence. We propose a debiased estimator through the Neyman orthogonality and establish its asymptotic normality under diverging horizons even when the behavior policy changes with time, as long as the nuisances have the statistical rates that can be achieved by many machine learning methods. We provide a concrete estimating procedure for these nuisances and show they can lead to valid inference. Synthetic experiments validate the numerical performance of our inference method, and we implement it in real-life decision-making problems, including bike repositioning and AI agentic tool use.
♻ ☆ Algorithmic Principles For Multiclass Learning Are Hard To Come By: Limits of Regularization and Proper Learning
Julian Asilis, Shaddin Dughmi, Vatsal Sharan, Alec Sun, Shang-Hua Teng, Chang Wang
Two of the most fundamental questions in statistical learning theory are the following: which prediction problems are learnable, and how should they be learned? For the former, elegant answers often take the form of combinatorial dimensions. The latter question, however, has proved considerably more elusive: all known general-purpose multiclass learners rely on intricate orientations of exponentially large one-inclusion structures, and familiar algorithmic principles such as proper learning and regularization remain poorly understood. Motivated by prior work, we ask whether learning reduces to proper learning---possibly over a larger hypothesis class---and whether proper or improper multiclass learning can ultimately be captured by suitable regularizers. Our primary results answer both questions negatively, resolving three open problems from prior work. First, we exhibit a learnable multiclass problem that cannot be embedded in any properly learnable class, meaning learning cannot be reduced to proper learning by enlarging the hypothesis class. Second, we demonstrate that proper learning can require training error and characterize this phenomenon precisely: every properly learnable class admits a proper learner making $o(m)$ errors on samples of size $m$, but every prescribed sublinear scale $a_m=o(m)$ is necessary for some properly learnable problem. Third, regularization is not a general learner: we exhibit a properly learnable class that cannot be learned by any Structural Risk Minimization (SRM) learner, and a learnable class that cannot be learned by any local regularizer. We complement these impossibility results with a positive theory that gives two sufficient conditions for SRM learnability and characterizes SRM representability through integrability of revealed preferences.

♻ ☆ Decoupling Distance and Networks: Hybrid Graph Attention-Geostatistical Methods for Spatio-temporal Risk Mapping
Toba Temitope Bamidele, Ezra Gayawan, Femi Barnabas Adebola, Olatunji Johnson
Accurate spatial prediction and rigorous uncertainty quantification are central to modern spatial epidemiology and environmental risk analysis. We introduce a statistically principled hybrid modelling framework that integrates the nonlinear, attention-based representation learning capabilities of a dynamic Graph Attention Network (GATv2) with a latent Gaussian spatial process from model-based geostatistics (MBG). This framework jointly captures relational dependence encoded in graph structures and continuous spatial dependence governed by physical proximity. We evaluate the proposed model via a controlled simulation study and an applied analysis of malaria prevalence data, comparing its predictive accuracy, calibration, and uncertainty quantification against classical geostatistical models and standalone GATv2 architectures. Our analyses show that GATv2 captures complex nonlinear interactions but fails to account for residual spatial autocorrelation, resulting in miscalibrated predictive distributions. Conversely, geostatistical models provide coherent uncertainty quantification through structured covariance functions yet are constrained by linear predictor assumptions and by their reliance on Euclidean distance to encode spatial structure. By integrating attention mechanisms and nonlinear features with an explicit probabilistic spatial random field, the hybrid model captured the relational dependence, consistently improved predictive accuracy, and provided more realistic uncertainty quantification in both simulation and applied settings. Overall, the findings demonstrate that the hybrid model constitutes a statistically coherent and empirically robust framework for modelling complex spatial and spatio-temporal processes in settings where both distance-based and structure-based dependencies operate.

♻ ☆ Recovery Theory for Projected Power Iterations in Permutation Synchronization

We study the projected power method for permutation synchronization: recovering $n$ unknown permutations of $m$ objects from pairwise relative permutations, observed independently with probability $p$ and independently corrupted by uniform permutations with probability $1-π_0$. Our main theorem establishes uniform one-step contraction for all estimates with optimally aligned block-error fraction at most $1/2-ε$, for fixed $ε>0$, including measurement-dependent estimates. When $np\ge C_0\log(n)$ and $m=o(npπ_0^2)$, one update contracts the error by a factor $O(m/(npπ_0^2))$, up to a floor of $O(e^{-c\min\{m\,npπ_0^2,\,npπ_0\}} + \log(n) / n)$. Thus, every initialization in this majority basin achieves $o(1)$ error after one update and maintains it uniformly over subsequent iterations. A reference-block spectral initializer enters the basin with probability $1-o(1)$, yielding end-to-end almost-exact recovery. If additionally $\min\{m\,npπ_0^2,\,npπ_0\} \ge C\log(n)$ for sufficiently large $C$, the method achieves exact recovery in finitely many iterations. We also establish prescribed-block recovery under weaker conditions for measurement-independent estimates and extend the guarantees to independent permutation-valued corruptions with uniform mean and to partial permutations with common visible support.

☆ Shrinkage prior for implicit generative models
Shreya Sinha-Roy, Christian P. Robert, Ritabrata Dutta
Implicit generative models based on deep neural networks have revolutionized many scientific fields, from weather research to language generation. They successfully model complex random objects arising in real-world problems. In this work, we propose a sample-efficient training mechanism for these models. Our approach leverages regularized inference with shrinkage priors and generalized Bayes. In the large $p$ (parameter dimension) and small $n$ (sample size) setting, sparsity-inducing priors have been successfully used for linear regression when $p \gg n$. However, their application to implicit generative models remains challenging due to the intractability of the likelihood function. To address this, we adapt a scoring rule posterior based on a strictly proper scoring rule, following the generalized Bayes framework. We then propose a block SGMCMC within Gibbs sampling mechanism. This enables efficient exploration of high-dimensional parameter spaces by identifying a sparse representation of neural implicit generative models. We demonstrate the performance of our proposed method through experiments on $p \gg n$ linear regression and an application of neural generative models.
☆ Post-stratified importance sampling
Yuling Yao, Sergei Tikhonov
Importance sampling is a building block of modern statistical computing, but the weighted estimate is prone to high or infinite variance. Moreover, its empirical standard error is often unreliable, leaving importance sampling without practical uncertainty quantification. Motivated by multilevel regression and poststratification (MRP) in survey sampling, we propose post-stratified importance sampling (PIS) for estimating target expectations from proposal draws. PIS reformulates arbitrarily high-dimensional weighting into two one-dimensional probabilistic modeling problems: regression for the conditional mean given the importance ratio and marginal density estimation for the importance ratio. Different modeling choices yield a family of PIS estimators, encompassing ordinary importance sampling as a special case. We develop a model-based implementation that combines one-dimensional Gaussian process regression for the conditional mean and score-informed heavy-tailed density estimation for the marginal law, using both the observed weights and the available density evaluations. We study the oracle gains of PIS and establish consistency under general and model-specific conditions. Simulations and applications to cross-validation demonstrate improvements in estimation accuracy and uncertainty quantification.

Inference in stochastic reaction-network models, such as the susceptible-exposed-infectious-recovered (SEIR) epidemic model, is crucial for understanding the dynamics of interacting systems in epidemiology, ecology, and systems biology. These models are typically represented as Markov jump processes (MJPs), with discrete, noisy observations and intractable likelihoods. Particle Markov chain Monte Carlo (PMCMC) offers a natural mechanism for inference on these hidden Markov models, but, even in moderate dimensional state spaces, particle degeneracy typically leads to poor mixing of the PMCMC algorithm. This paper focuses on improving the efficiency of particle Gibbs for inference on reaction networks by addressing the degeneracy problem. We focus on the $τ$-leap discretisation of the MJPs. The proposed method retains the exchangeability framework of xPG while adapting it to the structural and computational challenges specific to reaction networks. The new method is applied to several examples, including four coupled SEIR models, where it substantially improves mixing efficiency compared with standard particle Gibbs. In this example, xPG improves sample efficiency by more than an order of magnitude relative to standard particle Gibbs, making inference feasible in hours rather than weeks. As part of our tuning strategy, we provide a mechanism for tuning the number of particles that is applicable more generally, to any particle Gibbs algorithm.

While this is entirely a discrete probability model, a main challenge is the fitting of such a probabilistic graphical model due to the exponential intractability of normalizing constants within the Ising model. This model is applied to a five year sequence of weekly gun violence events across the 3109 counties of the continental United States to identify state changes in gun violence activity from 2021 to 2025.

☆ Enabling risk and reliability analysis in next-generation computational tools via multifidelity methods
Anirban Chaudhuri, Karen Willcox
Risk and reliability analysis are fundamental to the design, assessment, and operation of safety-critical complex systems; however, their integration into next-generation computational tools is constrained by the cost of uncertainty quantification with expensive computational models. The computational challenge is particularly prohibitive for tail-sensitive quantities, such as probabilities of failure, conditional values-at-risk, and buffered probabilities of failure, where accurate estimation can require a large number of model evaluations. Multifidelity methods provide a framework for addressing this computational bottleneck by combining information from models of varying accuracy and cost while retaining the predictive accuracy of the high-fidelity model. This review summarizes the state of the art in methods that enable scalable risk and reliability analysis using multifidelity control variates, multifidelity importance sampling, and multifidelity active learning.

Notably, our personalized policy fixes one assortment per customer type before the horizon and then offers every in-stock product within it, so it requires no dynamic re-optimization despite competing against the optimal fully adaptive policy. Finally, we construct instances in which optimal show-all revenue approaches only one-half of the fluid bound under deterministic arrivals and $1-w\approx0.4328567$ under IFR arrivals, where $we^w=1$. With an exact static assortment oracle, our IFR guarantee approaches the latter factor arbitrarily closely.

Such models cover discrete, continuous and functional data, as well as i.i.d. replicates of stochastic processes, but their likelihoods are often unavailable. In the recourse stage, $θ$ is frozen at the fitted $\tildeθ$, and a finite set of representative noise values $\{\bar x_j\}$ is pushed through the fitted mechanism to give model atoms $G(\tildeθ,\bar x_j)$. The held-out block optimizes weights $\textbf{w}$ on the model atoms to best match its own distribution. The optimized weights are then compared with theoretical weights under correct specification. Since each model atom is the image of known noise values, the disagreement between optimal and theoretical weights points to the part of the noise law that is wrong. The split makes the scaled weights conditionally multinomial, yielding a calibrated Pearson test. We prove strong consistency of both stages under checkable assumptions and illustrate the procedure on a Gaussian location--scale family, the number of segregating sites under Kingman's coalescent, a Yule process, and an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck diffusion.
♻ ☆ Product Monte Carlo: Expectation Under a Product of Densities
Pietro Carlotti, Sifan Liu, Yuling Yao
Aggregating independently computed sub-sample inferences is a well-known challenge in large-scale Bayesian computation, federated learning, and opinion pooling. The core problem is to approximate a distribution whose density is proportional to a product of individual densities. We propose Product Monte Carlo (PMC), an algorithm for computing arbitrary expectations under a product of densities using only Monte Carlo draws from individual densities. We turn the intractable product expectation into a regression problem by expressing it through a family of computable conditional expectations. Besides the point estimate, our fully Bayesian regression formulation provides coherent uncertainty quantification and principled diagnostics. We establish theoretical guarantees on consistency and characterize convergence rates for the PMC estimator. Across simulated and real-data experiments varying the number, dimensionality, and heterogeneity of the component distributions, PMC achieves higher estimation accuracy, better-calibrated uncertainty coverage, and improved scalability at a lower computational cost than existing methods. In addition, PMC requires no density evaluation, making it applicable to simulation-based inference, as we demonstrate in an application with protein images.
♻ ☆ Generalized and Scalable Deep Gaussian Process Emulation
Deyu Ming, Daniel Williamson
Gaussian process (GP) emulators have become essential tools for approximating complex simulators, significantly reducing computational demands in optimization, sensitivity analysis, and model calibration. While traditional GP emulators effectively model continuous and Gaussian-distributed simulator outputs with homogeneous variability, they typically struggle with discrete, heteroskedastic Gaussian, or non-Gaussian data, limiting their applicability to increasingly common stochastic simulators. A scalable Generalized Deep Gaussian Process (GDGP) emulation framework is introduced to accommodate simulators with heteroskedastic Gaussian outputs and a wide range of non-Gaussian response distributions, including Poisson, negative binomial, and categorical distributions. The GDGP framework leverages the expressiveness of DGPs and extends them to latent GP structures, enabling it to capture the complex, non-stationary behavior inherent in many simulators while also modeling non-Gaussian simulator outputs. GDGP is made scalable by incorporating the Vecchia approximation for settings with a large number of input locations, while also developing efficient inference procedures for handling large numbers of replicates. In particular, methodological developments are presented that further enhance the computation of the approach for heteroskedastic Gaussian responses. A series of synthetic and empirical examples demonstrates that these extensions deliver the practical application of GDGP emulators and a unified methodology capable of addressing diverse modeling challenges. The proposed GDGP framework is implemented in the open-source R package dgpsi.
